One-read compound queries force answer-specific cells and exponentially costly updates; one-bit, order-independent updates instead force fact-specific cells. At minimum storage capacity, a robust counterpart holds: when update stretch is averaged uniformly over all semantic cube edges, small excess stretch bounds expected distance from a coordinate encoding under the uniform content distribution. It also bounds the information inaccessible to a one-read consumer. Preservation imposes further constraints. On a common invariant ready-state domain, old content preserved by ordinary zero-read overwrites must factor through the unwritten coordinates. Distributed encodings can require reading every cell to choose a preserving update. For conditional Horn reasoning, we obtain a second pair of exact endpoints: maintaining answers makes use local, while minimum storage and one-change named revision force a rule vector whose optimal query-read cost is determined exactly. These results explain how acquired distinctions, subsequent uses, and update constraints jointly determine the costs and organization of a retained resource.

articles.title: The Presupposition Problem in Representation Genesis
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.21745v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models are the first systems to achieve high cognitive performance without clearly undergoing representation genesis: the transition from a non-representing physical system to one whose states guide behavior in a content-sensitive way. Prior cognitive systems had already made this transition before we could examine it, and philosophy of mind treated genesis as a background condition rather than an explanatory target. LLMs provide a case that does not clearly involve this transition, making the genesis question newly urgent: if genesis did not occur, which cognitive capacities are affected, and why? We currently lack the conceptual resources to answer this. The reason, this paper argues, is structural. Major frameworks in philosophy of mind, including the Language of Thought hypothesis, teleosemantics, predictive processing, enactivism, and genetic phenomenology, share a common feature when applied to the genesis question: at some explanatory step, each deploys concepts whose explanatory purchase depends on the system already being organized as a representer. This pattern, which we call the Representation Presupposition structure, generates systematic explanatory deferral. Attempts to explain the first acquisition of content-manipulable representation within the existing categorical vocabulary import resources from the representational side of the transition itself. We call this the Representation Regress. The paper offers a conceptual diagnosis rather than a new theory, establishing the structure of the problem and deriving two minimum adequacy conditions for any account that avoids this pattern. LLMs make the absence of such a theory consequential rather than merely theoretical.

articles.title: SYN-DIGITS: A Synthetic Control Framework for Calibrated Digital Twin Simulation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2604.07513v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Persona simulation based on large language models---often referred to as digital twin simulation---is increasingly used for market research, recommender systems, and social science research. However, these simulations often exhibit systematic bias and miscalibration relative to real human behavior. We propose SYN-DIGITS, a model-agnostic, post-hoc calibration framework that learns relationships among questions from digital twins and transfers them to predict human responses. We focus on a cold-start setting in which no human response to the target question is observed, so calibration must rely on digital twins and human data on reference questions. Our analysis shows that, though digital twins may not reproduce individual human responses accurately, they can capture nontrivial relationships among questions that can be effectively transferred to the human side. When individual-level data is unavailable and we only have access to marginal information on reference questions, our framework also supports distribution-level calibration for predicting the distribution of human responses on the target question. Across three datasets and thirteen persona constructions, experiments show that SYN-DIGITS achieves 11% to 417% relative improvements in individual-level correlation and 46%--57% relative reductions in distributional discrepancy compared to uncalibrated baselines.

articles.title: Anthropogenic Regional Adaptation in Multimodal Vision-Language Model
articles.summary:
arXiv:2604.11490v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: While the field of vision-language (VL) has achieved remarkable success in integrating visual and textual information across multiple languages and domains, there is still no dedicated framework for assessing human-centric alignment in vision-language systems. We offer two contributions to address this gap. First, we introduce Anthropogenic Regional Adaptation: a novel paradigm that aims to optimize model relevance to specific regional contexts while ensuring the retention of global generalization capabilities. Second, we present a simple, but effective adaptation method named Geographical-generalization-made-easy (GG-EZ), which utilizes regional data filtering and model merging. Through comprehensive experiments on 3 VL architectures: large vision-language models, text-to-image diffusion models, and vision-language embedding models, and a case study in Southeast Asia (SEA) regional adaptation, we demonstrate the importance of Anthropogenic Regional Adaptation and the effectiveness of GG-EZ, showing 5-15% gains in cultural relevance metrics across SEA while maintaining over 98% of global performance and even occasionally surpassing it. Our findings establish Anthropogenic Regional Alignment as a foundational paradigm towards applicability of multimodal vision-language models in diverse regions and demonstrate a simple-yet-effective baseline method that optimizes regional value alignment while preserving global generalization.

articles.title: Foundation Models to Unlock Real-World Evidence from Nationwide Medical Claims
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.02740v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Real-world data increasingly inform regulatory and clinical decisions. Administrative claims, among their major sources, continuously track care and its cost across providers throughout enrollment, yet remain largely unexplored for healthcare foundation models. Here we present ReClaim, a family of generative foundation models built on 43.8 billion claims records from more than 200 million enrollees in the MarketScan Research Databases. ReClaim learns diagnoses, procedures, medications and expenditure jointly through pre-training from scratch, then specializes for downstream prediction tasks through post-training, with a training cutoff at the end of 2022. In predicting more than 1,000 diseases, ReClaim achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.769, outperforming disease-specific gradient-boosted models (0.663) and a transformer-based baseline (0.694), and retained this advantage when generalizing to two independent cross-domain electronic health record datasets. ReClaim also outperformed gradient-boosted models in forecasting next-year expenditure and in identifying high-need, high-cost enrollees. ReClaim maintained its advantage in disease prediction and expenditure forecasting on post-cutoff data (2023-2024). Beyond prediction, ReClaim representations used as covariates resulted in improved effect estimates compared with algorithm-derived covariates, when benchmarked against results expected from randomized controlled trials. Together, these results establish nationwide insurance claims as a scalable substrate for healthcare foundation models supporting disease prediction, expenditure forecasting and confounding adjustment in real-world evidence studies. Code is available at https://github.com/BIDS-Xu-Lab/ReClaim.

articles.title: Pacing Branch Parallelism in LLM Serving
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.06914v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent methods expose intra-request parallelism in LLM outputs, allowing independent branches to decode concurrently. Existing serving systems execute these branches eagerly or under fixed caps. We show that both are brittle: eager admission inflates the shared decode step, degrading co-batched requests in serial stages, while conservative fixed caps forgo the throughput that motivated exposing branches in the first place. We call the excess step latency caused by admitted branches the \emph{branch externality} and show that the safe width depends on batch composition, context lengths, and accumulated slack, all of which change continuously over a workload trace. We introduce PACE, a per-step admission controller that treats extra branches as opportunistic width, admitted only when the predicted branch externality fits within the batch's current slack budget. Per-step regulation is practical because branch-level scheduling decouples compute from memory: branches share the request's prefix KV, so expanding or contracting width requires no memory reclamation. On Qwen3-32B, PACE improves goodput by $1.77\times$ over serving without branch parallelism and by $1.48\times$ over eager admission while maintaining 99\% SLO attainment. Comparable gains ($1.72$--$2.15\times$) hold on five additional dense and mixture-of-experts models with up to 671B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/Swapnil-Gandhi/PACE

articles.title: MulTaBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Tabular Learning with Text and Image
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.10616v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models have recently established the state of the art in supervised tabular learning, by leveraging pretraining to learn generalizable representations of numerical and categorical structured data. However, they lack native support for unstructured modalities such as text and image, and rely on frozen, pretrained embeddings to process them. On established Multimodal Tabular Learning benchmarks, we show that tuning the embeddings to the task improves performance. Existing benchmarks, however, often focus on the mere co-occurrence of modalities; this leads to high variance across datasets and masks the benefits of task-specific tuning. To address this gap, we introduce MulTaBench, a benchmark of 40 datasets, split equally between image-tabular and text-tabular tasks. We focus on predictive tasks where the modalities provide complementary predictive signal, and where generic embeddings lose critical information, necessitating Target-Aware Representations that are aligned with the task. Our experimental results demonstrate that the gains from target-aware representation tuning generalize across both text and image modalities, several tabular learners, encoder scales, and embedding dimensions. MulTaBench constitutes the largest image-tabular benchmarking effort to date, spanning high-impact domains such as healthcare and e-commerce. It is designed to enable the research of novel architectures which incorporate joint modeling and target-aware representations, paving the way for the development of novel Multimodal Tabular Foundation Models.

articles.title: Mobius Injection: From One-Shot Prompt Injection to Sustained Resource Exhaustion in AI Agent Infrastructure
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.11442v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have emerged as key intermediaries, orchestrating complex interactions between human users and a wide range of digital services and LLM infrastructures. While prior research has extensively examined the security of LLMs and agents in isolation, the systemic risk of the agent acting as a disruptive "hub" within the user-agent-service chain remains largely overlooked. In this work, we expose a novel threat paradigm by introducing Mobius Injection, a sophisticated attack that weaponizes autonomous agents into zombie nodes to launch what we define as Agent-based and -Oriented DDoS (AbO-DDoS) attacks. Mobius Injection composes known indirect prompt injection and persistent agent components through a distinct structural mechanism named Semantic Closure, which induces sustained recursive execution of agent components through a single injection event. We demonstrate that this attack is lightweight for the adversary, can evade traditional volumetric DDoS monitors and input filters calibrated for low false-positive rates, and is highly configurable, allowing for surgical targeting of specific environments or model providers. To evaluate the real-world impact, we conduct extensive experiments across three representative claw-style agents and three mainstream coding agents, integrated with 12 frontier proprietary or open-weight LLMs. Our results demonstrate that Mobius Injection achieves substantial attack success across diverse tasks, driving single-node call amplification up to 51.0x. Under coordinated multi-node pressure, each infected node still drains about 123k--127k tokens on a shared five-GPU backend; benign request latency rises by abou 23x--24x, and coordinated infections eventually saturate shared capacity until benign traffic is effectively denied service.

articles.title: Two is better than one: A Collapse-free Multi-Reward RLIF Training Framework
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.22620v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning ability of LLMs, but often depends on external supervision from human annotations or gold-standard solutions. Reinforcement learning from internal feedback (RLIF) has recently emerged as a scalable unsupervised alternative, using signals extracted from the model itself. However, existing RLIF methods typically rely on a single internal reward, which can lead to reward hacking, entropy collapse, and degraded reasoning structure. We propose a multi-reward RLIF framework that decomposes the training signal into two complementary components: an answer-level reward based on cluster voting and a completion-level reward based on token-wise self-certainty. To combine these signals robustly, we apply GDPO-based normalization to reduce reward-scale imbalance. We further introduce KL-Cov regularization, which targets low-entropy token distributions responsible for disproportionate entropy reduction, preserving exploration and preventing late-stage collapse. Across mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, our method improves stability and robustness over prior unsupervised RL approaches, while achieving performance close to supervised RLVR methods. These results show that complementary internal rewards, combined with targeted regularization, can support stable long-horizon reasoning without relying on external ground-truth supervision. Code will be released soon.

articles.title: Rubric-Guided Process Reward for Stepwise Model Routing
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.29310v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Stepwise model routing improves the efficiency of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) by assigning each reasoning step to a suitable model. Recent methods formulate routing as a sequential decision process and train the router with reinforcement learning. However, although they model routing as a process, they still supervise the router with outcome rewards. Such rewards only reflect final answer correctness and fail to evaluate intermediate routing decisions, which can weaken performance and generalization. To address this gap, we propose RoRo, a rubric-guided process reward framework for stepwise model routing. RoRo first collects diverse routing trajectories and constructs preference pairs based on outcome, cost, and process quality. It then trains a Rubricor to generate a query-specific evaluation rubric and a Judge to score routing trajectories under this rubric through alternating optimization. The resulting process rewards are combined with outcome rewards to optimize the routing policy via GRPO. Experiments on five reasoning benchmarks under both same-family and cross-family settings show that RoRo consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves better accuracy and cost trade-offs.

articles.title: Selective Linkage Precision for Released Medical Vision-Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.02276v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Hospitals may release de-identified chest radiographs while restricting access to their reports. An attacker who already has reports from the same population and their metadata can use a vision-language model (VLM) to match images to reports. We introduce selective linkage precision, which measures correct matches among the highest-confidence queries after filtering candidates by the available attributes. Across 8 public VLMs and 3 chest radiograph datasets, the maximum whole-pool Recall@1 is 0.40%. However, this metric averages over every query without attribute filtering. On ReXGradient-160K, MedSigLIP-448 reaches 67.68% precision at a budget of 100 after filtering by sex, age band, and projection, with a median of 327 candidate reports. On the same eligible query set, an attribute-only policy reaches 24.99% and the model alone reaches 1.98%. Adding acquisition year, available in only 1 of the 3 datasets, yields 99.05% precision and a median of 24 candidates. Uniform guessing on the observed selected queries has an expected precision of 19.91%. Expanding the primary-setting collection to all 123,100 ReXGradient studies lowers precision to 37.23%. On BioViL-T, the tested head finetuning procedures do not lower linkage below the public checkpoint. Selective linkage precision requires inference without retraining and could help hospitals evaluate which attributes to publish.

articles.title: Do Neural Retrievers Prefer Certain Documents? Evidence of Learned Relevance Priors
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.02814v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Neural retrievers are trained to estimate query-document relevance from annotated query-document pairs. Yet annotation protocols may not purely reflect relevance: they select only a subset of documents for labeling, and this selection can favor certain document types over others. We investigate whether supervised bi-encoder retrievers implicitly learn a document-level relevance prior: a query-independent signal encoded in their representation space as a side effect of training on annotated data. We estimate this prior by training simple classifiers on frozen document embeddings and evaluate three state-of-the-art retrievers across multiple IR benchmarks. We find that supervised neural retrievers encode relevance priors that generalize to unseen documents and are consistent across models. These priors are associated with a findability gap: documents with lower prior are systematically harder to retrieve, even when genuinely relevant. This effect appears in supervised dense retrievers but is weaker and less consistent in BM25, and it persists under controlled matched-document comparisons. Using LLM-based explanations, we find that judged-relevant documents tend to be comprehensive, self-contained summaries of mainstream topics, while niche, fragmentary, or highly technical content is often left unjudged. Retrievers appear to internalize this bias, ranking documents with these favored features higher than documents that lack them, independently of their actual relevance. Our findings expose a structural limitation of supervised retrieval: models trained on annotated data do not just learn relevance, but also the implicit document preferences in their training data.

articles.title: Humans' ALMANAC: A Human Collaboration Dataset of Action-Level Mental Model Annotations for Agent Collaboration
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.06388v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent advances in LLM agents have enabled complex cognitive capabilities, such as multi-step reasoning, planning, and tool use, that increasingly position these agents as collaborative partners in human workflows. Effective collaboration, however, requires collaborators to continuously maintain and align mental models of their own reasoning, partners' intentions, and shared goals during the collaborative process. Today's agents rarely develop such capabilities since they are primarily optimized for task completion rather than for maintaining the underlying mental models required for collaborative processes. Moreover, the community lacks authentic human collaboration data with action-level mental model annotations that could guide agents toward collaborative competence. To bridge this gap, we present ALMANAC, a dataset of Action-Level Mental model ANnotations for Agent Collaboration built from the Map Task, a classic dyadic routing task from social science. ALMANAC contains 2,987 collaboration actions, each paired with theory-informed mental model annotations that record the participants' self-reasoning, perceived partner intent, and perceived team goal. We benchmark six LLMs on predicting humans' next-turn behavior and mental models. Our results demonstrate ALMANAC's utility in evaluating models' ability to simulate human collaborative behaviors and infer their underlying mental models. The project page is available at https://human-agent-collab.hailab.io/almanac.

articles.title: TRACER: Token ReAssignment for Concept ERasure in Generative Recommendation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.07688v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Generative recommendation formulates next-item prediction as autoregressive generation over semantic ID (SID) sequences derived from users' historical interactions, making modern recommender systems structurally similar to large language models (LLMs). As privacy and safety concerns grow, these systems increasingly require concept unlearning to remove sensitive or harmful concepts associated with items. However, existing LLM unlearning methods cannot be directly applied to generative recommendation. Unlike word tokens with explicit semantics, SIDs are abstract identifiers that are often shared by both forget and retain items, leading to severe conflicts between concept removal and recommendation utility preservation.
  To address this challenge, we propose TRACER, an end-to-end concept unlearning framework based on token reassignment. Rather than directly suppressing shared SIDs, TRACER reassigns concept-related items to alternative tokens that better facilitate forgetting while minimizing side effects on retained items. We further introduce a coherence regularizer to preserve semantic consistency among retain items during unlearning. Experiments on real-world recommendation datasets demonstrate that TRACER effectively removes target concepts while substantially better preserving recommendation utility than existing unlearning baselines.

articles.title: Paediatric-HGNN: A Hybrid Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Detecting Disfluency in Children's Speech via Multiscale Acoustic Fusion
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.08210v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Automated stuttering detection (ASD) systems struggle with paediatric speech due to high acoustic variability in developing voices and the subtle distinction between pathological stuttering and typical developmental disfluencies. We introduce Paediatric-HGNN, a framework using a Context-aware Part-whole Interaction Network (CaPIN) tailored for paediatric data. Instead of conventional 1D signal modelling, our approach builds a heterogeneous graph capturing hierarchical relationships between lexical units (word nodes) and fine-grained acoustic segments (frame nodes). Trained on curated paediatric corpora (UCLASS and FluencyBank), Paediatric-HGNN achieves 82.4% weighted accuracy and a Typical Disfluency F1-score of 0.386. Modelling hierarchical lexical-acoustic interactions captures developmental "searching" behaviour, offering a more robust and interpretable tool for early clinical intervention.

articles.title: When No Answer Is Correct: Diagnosing Absent Answer Detection for MLLMs in Video Understanding
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.08239v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made substantial advancements in video understanding, yet the reliability of their responses remains underexplored. This work presents a diagnostic study of absent answer detection for MLLMs in video understanding, where the correct answer is deliberately excluded from the candidate set and a reliable model is expected to recognize that no valid option exists. We evaluate the absent answer detection behavior under three settings: multiple-choice questions augmented with a ``None of the Above'' option, open-ended generation with a detection instruction, and standard evaluation without any guidance. Across a diverse set of models and benchmarks, we find that MLLMs overwhelmingly select plausible distractors rather than detecting the absent answer. This failure is more pronounced in temporal reasoning tasks and worsens with denser frame sampling. We further explore chain-of-thought prompting as a mitigation strategy and find that while it substantially improves detection rates, performance remains unsatisfactory, suggesting that prompting-based strategies alone are insufficient to fully address this limitation. These findings expose a systematic failure in absent answer detection and highlight the need for explicit detection mechanisms in multimodal systems.

articles.title: Detecting Historical Turning Points in Italian Media: A Complex Systems Approach to a Diachronic News Corpus
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.14348v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Introduction: The increasing availability of large-scale textual corpora has opened new possibilities for data-driven, quantitative approaches to historical analysis using Natural Language Processing (NLP). However, diachronic corpora with historical relevance from the pre-digital era remain scarce and often incomplete.
  Methods: We present a quantitative approach to historical analysis based on the reconstruction and exploration of a diachronic corpus of around 600,000 articles from the Italian newspaper "La Repubblica", covering all the articles published from the first of January 1985 to the 31st of December 2000 - a period of major political, social, and geopolitical change in Italy and globally. Using NLP techniques, we analyze the text at both lexical and semantic levels; we then apply tools from complex systems and statistical physics to trace shifts in media discourse over time.
  Results: The word usage in the corpus is bursty, with a heavy-tailed distribution of Fano factors that is robust across timescales. Changepoints in word salience and the block structure of semantic similarity allow us to detect key transition periods, such as the transition from the First Republic to the Second Republic in Italy, or major international conflicts like the Gulf War or the Kosovo War, without relying on prior labeling. Periods of war correspond to lower entropy in the semantic space, indicating a more focused discourse.
  Discussion: The results show how combining computational linguistics with ideas from complex systems can offer new quantitative insight into historical changes, opening up new paths for studying the dynamics of media and society through large-scale textual data.

articles.title: SWE-Opt: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Performance-Oriented Repository-Level Optimization
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.25530v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Software performance optimization is a notoriously complex and manual task. Despite the growing use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for code refinement, we still lack benchmarks that capture how optimization actually happens in real-world codebases. Existing frameworks often oversimplify the problem by focusing on isolated functions or a single performance metric, missing the critical trade-offs between execution time and memory footprint, the inherent noise of the measurement environment, and the variability introduced by different input data and execution conditions. We address this by introducing SWE-Opt, a repository-level benchmark derived from 102 expert-written optimizations from open-source projects. Unlike previous benchmarks, SWE-Opt pairs each task with parameterized tests to evaluate runtime, peak memory, and Time-Weighted Memory Usage (TWMU) across varying input data and execution conditions under noise-aware measurement conditions. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs struggle significantly: runtime gains are sparse and inconsistent, and memory optimizations are nearly non-existent. An agentic setting with iterative repository exploration improves patch correctness substantially but does not translate into performance gains. This stands in sharp contrast to expert implementations, which achieve an aggregate speedup of 15.5x and peak memory reduction of 171.3x over benchmark tasks. Expert-written improvements are observed in 93.1% of tasks for runtime and 70.6% for peak memory. Our findings expose a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the demands of expert-level engineering.

articles.title: fog: Generating Expressive Motion through Layered Function Composition of Code for Heider-Simmel Animation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.07952v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Motion and emotion are core parts of intelligent, expressive behavior. In this paper, we introduce fog, a layered function composition framework for generating motion functions. We demonstrate how fog can be used to express motion and emotion in Heider-Simmel style animations. This code generation framework can help users generate functions for verbs, adverbs, and emotions to capture the trajectory, manner, and feeling of motion. It is complemented by an animation editor that helps users provide spatial context in the form of marks, arrows, and paths. We evaluate our approach with a technical evaluations investigating different function generation and composition setups. In a mixed-methods user study (n=12), we find that fog can support users can support users by relaying spatial context they mark and draw and giving them more dimensions for control.

articles.title: Query Language Sensitivity in Automated Sentiment Scores of LLM Responses
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.13304v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Automated scores are often used to summarize how large language models describe brands across prompts, providers, and languages. Such scores can vary because the answers differ, because the scoring instrument behaves differently across texts or languages, or for both reasons. We examine this measurement problem in 12,933 responses from a design crossing 20 stored brand labels, eight query languages, three provider aliases, and 15 prompt identifiers. The outcome is the signed winning-class confidence from a multilingual sentiment classifier: neutral winners are coded zero, while positive and negative winners receive signed confidence. A crossed linear mixed model fitted to all responses assigns 26.49% of fitted variance to query language and 1.46% to brand. An exploratory refit after excluding English assigns 5.07% to language and 2.23% to brand. These percentages have different denominators: total fitted variance falls by 65.08%, and absolute brand variance falls by 46.65%. English contains 591 negative classifier scores among 1,620 answers, compared with 77 among 11,313 answers in the other seven languages. The result shows that the original variance decomposition is highly sensitive to English inclusion. It does not identify a causal English effect or establish that English answers are more negative toward the brands. The classifier was trained for tweet sentiment, receives no separate target-brand condition, and English is the only study language represented in its documented sentiment fine-tuning set. Automated score differences should therefore be checked as properties of both the answers and the measurement instrument before they guide substantive conclusions.

articles.title: Memory Efficient Audio Synthesis with Decoupled Temporal Depth Diffusion Transformers
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.23811v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Siri Expressive Voices synthesize rich, configurable speech in real time and entirely on device, powered by AFM 3 Core Advanced, Apple's most powerful on-device foundation model. This work presents the memory-efficient audio synthesis architecture behind that capability: a detokenizer that converts the semantic audio tokens emitted by the foundation model into high-fidelity audio within the tight compute and memory budget of the Scalable Matrix Extension (SME). We convert semantic audio tokens to a residual vector quantization (RVQ) representation with a three-component design, a streaming encoder, a temporal decoder, and a depth decoder, that systematically decouples temporal and depth processing. A single reusable depth decoder with Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-style stage conditioning generates all RVQ levels autoregressively, replacing the dedicated per-level decoders of prior multi-decoder architectures, while causal sliding window attention with fixed-window key-value caching yields constant memory complexity independent of sequence length. Deployed on the AMX, the detokenizer sustains roughly 10 ms per generation step, about 16x faster than real time, with a peak runtime memory of only 21 MB and 329 MB of on-device assets, enabling continuous streaming synthesis of 20-320 seconds of audio. This constant, small footprint replaces the linear and quadratic memory scaling of conventional transformer- and GAN-based approaches. Ablation studies validate the key architectural components, and audio quality assessment confirms that the architecture maintains synthesis fidelity while achieving efficiency gains over existing methods. Operating at a 1-billion-parameter activation size within AFM 3 Core Advanced, it improves Mean Opinion Score by +0.28 overall (4.15 vs. 3.87) and by +0.42 on conversational speech (4.24 vs. 3.82) over the prior on-device text-to-speech system.

articles.title: ClinFusion: A Vision-Centric Multimodal LLM System for Holistic Medical Understanding
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.24743v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) hold immense potential to revolutionize clinical practice, yet deploying them in the medical domain is fundamentally a vision-centric challenge: models must absorb knowledge from heterogeneous 2D and 3D medical images, and evaluation protocols must align with radiologists' clinical practice and provide an accurate, fine-grained and factualness-driven assessment. In this paper, we introduce ClinFusion, a vision-centric MLLM designed for holistic medical understanding that systematically addresses these limitations. We propose a compositional and cascaded vision encoder architecture featuring a Cascade Spatial-Aware Locality Fusion operator that unifies diverse 2D and native 3D medical image understanding within a fused encoder. We further introduce a vision-grounded evaluation framework, including MedIF-Bench for instruction-following assessment and a region-of-interest-grounded method for clinically aligned and factualness-driven report generation evaluation. We show that ClinFusion sets a new state-of-the-art across a comprehensive suite of 2D and 3D multimodal medical benchmarks---spanning visual question answering, report generation, and instruction following---as well as textual medical tasks, outperforming leading open-source medical MLLMs (\textit{e.g.}, Hulu-Med, Lingshu) on 20 out of 24 benchmarks and demonstrating multimodal capabilities better than powerful proprietary models such as GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Flash on 13 out of 16 benchmarks, and can be further augmented with agentic tool use for retrieval-augmented and tool-assisted clinical workflows. A blinded evaluation by board-certified radiologists confirms that ClinFusion produces the highest-ranked reports, and validates our RoI-grounded metric as achieving the strongest correlation with expert judgment among all automatic evaluation metrics examined.

articles.title: MediaWiki Code2Code Search: Neural Retrieval for the Semantic Discovery of Open-Source Software Entities
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.26766v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Code search in large-scale ecosystems is often hindered by the lexical gap between user queries and implementation details, alongside the trade-off between the low latency of traditional Information Retrieval (IR) and the precision of Deep Learning (DL). We present MediaWiki Code2Code Search, a neural retrieval system for semantic code-to-code discovery. By indexing 1.29 million structural entities (functions, types, and templates) across 2,500+ MediaWiki repositories, our system enables retrieval based on computational intent rather than surface tokens. We employ a split-build architecture, decoupling GPU-intensive offline indexing from a CPU-only serving layer; our FAISS IVF-PQ index occupies 168.6 MiB: a 96.6\% reduction compared to a flat float32 baseline, and achieves a median query latency of 1.85 seconds on commodity hardware, satisfying the 6 GiB RAM constraint of Wikimedia Toolforge. In a blinded evaluation graded by a three-model LLM jury (inter-judge Krippendorff's $\alpha = 0.74$), our system improves ranking quality over a BM25 baseline across a 27-query benchmark, raising the jury-mean nDCG@10 (to 0.81 from 0.63), a positive and consistent gain across all judges. Gains are most pronounced in name-obfuscated and cross-language tasks where lexical methods fail. The system is available at https://code2codesearch.toolforge.org under the Apache 2.0 licence and provides an open RESTful API.

articles.title: AgentSnare: Learning to Delay, Divert, and Defuse Autonomous Web Penetration Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.26998v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language model agents automate web penetration testing through observation-action loops, enabling defenders to influence decisions with deceptive decoy observations. Advanced agents can recognize and bypass static decoys, then refocus on real targets. We propose AgentSnare, a trajectory-adaptive deception system that expands a decoy environment alongside exploration. For online deployment, ShadowOS combines an LLM-driven decoy constructor with a virtual kernel. Conditioned on exploration, it generates decoy artifacts that the kernel materializes and handles consistently across interactions, sustaining long-horizon exploration. Because deploying a powerful LLM for decoy construction is costly and slow, we train a small LLM using an offline adversarial interaction-simulation framework. It synthesizes multi-round trajectories by generating candidates and retaining those that sustain simulated interactions. Across 15 CVE-Bench web applications and four attacker models, AgentSnare absorbs 49.9% of tool calls to delay attacks, retains 57.2% of post-entry actions in the decoy to divert trajectories, and grounds 89.5% of completion reports in decoy evidence to defuse threats; across 60 attacker-CVE pairs, no real target is exploited at pass@3.

articles.title: Wrong but Useful: Trajectory Value Beyond Answer Correctness in Multi-Agent Messages
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.14375v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A solution can end with a wrong answer and still help another solver. In multi-agent reasoning, evaluating only a message's proposed answer can therefore miss its contribution to the receiver. We measure this contribution as trajectory value: the change in a fixed integrator's probability of answering correctly when a cached message is present rather than removed. Controlled replay across five benchmarks and two model families separates message effects from identical-input variation. The strongest evidence is for Gemma: in a pre-registered fresh-call re-test, 34 of 73 selected wrong-answer messages pass individual confirmation, exceeding control-calibrated upper bounds on expected false confirmations of 11.4--20.8. The finding is benchmark-dependent and the conservative criterion no longer passes without SciBench. A blinded two-author audit supports the selected answer labels, while neutral replacements show that the helpful effect is not explained solely by message length and position. On held-out replay blocks of the same problems, a message-specific removal rule improves accuracy over the strongest tested correctness-only rule by 1.61 percentage points [1.01, 2.25]. Post hoc analysis localizes most of this gap to pools containing no correct proposal. Evidence for gpt-oss is weaker, and the tested predictors do not establish a practical way to identify useful errors in advance. The results support measuring answer correctness and receiver benefit separately, with value understood as conditional on the message pool, receiver and generation format.

articles.title: RAP: Research Attention Prediction in Language Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.10092v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: LLM agents increasingly support research planning and execution, where judgments about current and anticipated research activity inform decisions. Yet whether they can infer changes across a whole field from the partial evidence they retrieve through online scholarly search remains unclear. We introduce Research Attention Prediction (RAP), a literature search benchmark for evaluating this ability. We build a local search environment from 356,357 dated arXiv papers and construct two complementary evaluation tasks. The benchmark comprises a Core set of 2,160 questions across 54 AI/ML fields and an Extended set covering 269 fields. Our evaluation and analysis of LLM agents show that search substantially improves stronger agents' recognition of recent changes, while forecasting gains remain limited or negative. Agents update forecasts across dates and adjust their investigations to forecasting goals, but these adaptations do not reliably yield accurate predictions of future shifts. Even for recent changes, final judgments can diverge from what the retrieved papers indicate. These findings show that agents can recognise some recent changes, yet reliably anticipating future research activity remains difficult despite changes in their answers and investigations.

articles.title: EvoOntology: A Self-Evolving Ontology Layer for Data Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.15779v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Data agents aim to fulfill natural-language instructions over heterogeneous data, including tables, files, and databases. However, data agents face a challenging agent-data gap: heterogeneous data resides outside the agent, while the agent can access it (e.g., column names and file paths) only through generic tools. Existing approaches either let agents directly explore raw data sources or inject manually constructed semantic layers into prompts. However, neither scales well to large heterogeneous data sources nor adapts to different agent behaviors. In this paper, we introduce EvoOntology, a self-evolving ontology layer for data agents. EvoOntology encapsulates the ontology as an MCP server comprising a schema layer, a content layer, and a tool layer, enabling agents to actively query and interact with the ontology at runtime. To this end, we introduce a builder agent for autonomous ontology construction and a self-evolution loop that continuously refines the ontology through attribution-guided typed edits that are accepted only after a backbone-conditional paired evaluation. Experiments on three well-adopted data-agent benchmarks with four LLM backbones demonstrate that EvoOntology consistently outperforms strong baselines and existing semantic-layer approaches, effectively bridging the agent-data gap and enabling more effective interaction with heterogeneous data. Code: https://github.com/ruc-datalab/EvoOntology

articles.title: Using OCR Heads to Verbalize Image Semantics
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.18823v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: How do VLMs map from pixels to semantics? To understand this general question, we focus on a narrow one: studying how VLMs perform optical character recognition (OCR). Across four models, we identify attention heads causally necessary for OCR, and discover that these are in fact general-purpose heads that output interpretable semantic features across all image tokens. For example, pointing these heads at an image token containing the word "bike" causes Qwen3-VL-8B to output "bike," but pointing them at a bird wing causes the model to output the token "feathers." We collapse these heads' attention weights into a single verbalization lens transformation that reveals interpretable semantic features in hidden states across all layers. When combined with projection to vocabulary space, we can obtain interpretable labels starting from layer 0, showing that image representations are in fact aligned with language in early layers. We find that we can also use the inverse of this transformation to edit non-word concepts, e.g., replacing a tractor with a revolver in a naturalistic image, providing causal evidence that this subspace is useful for more than just OCR. Our results are an example of how the study of specific mechanisms can shed light on broader interpretability problems.

articles.title: Beyond Outcome Rewards: Post-Rationale Distribution Optimization for Selective Prediction in Reasoning Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.38850v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Reasoning models are trained to produce correct answers, yet selective deployment requires ranking which answers to accept or defer, and outcome-reward training does not directly optimize the post-rationale distribution used for that decision. We identify two mismatches: expected correctness is mode-seeking rather than distribution-eliciting, and scoring an average across rationales rewards disagreement unavailable to a single-rationale decision. We introduce Post-Rationale Distribution Optimization (PRDO), which applies a proper score to the answer distribution after each sampled rationale, without target rationales or separate confidence labels. Across four 0.6--3.8-billion-parameter models on MMLU-Pro, PRDO improves Brier score, error ranking and secondary accuracy relative to budget-matched, temperature-scaled GRPO. At 20\% realized error, oracle coverage rises by \npj{Q3a_vs_grpo.qwen3-0.6b.mp.oracle_cov@0.2.ppabs}--\npj{Q3a_vs_grpo.phi-4-mini.mp.oracle_cov@0.2.ppabs} percentage points, and ranking gains transfer to unseen tasks. Matched controls identify proper, per-rationale scoring as the active design choices, while verification tasks show the boundary: better selective ranking can coexist with lower full-coverage accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/ZimmyGao/openjev-rlcd

articles.title: Parsed Text Understates Vision-Language Models: From Below to Above Expert Agreement on Fine-Grained Facial Emotion
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.08162v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: EmoNet-Face-HQ is a benchmark of 2,500 generated portraits, each rated by four psychology experts on 40 emotion categories. It concludes that vision-language models (VLMs) on average offer no dependable improvement over random guessing and that a fine-tuned model is required. The benchmark reads each model's answer from generated text, and its zero-shot prompt demands a fixed number of emotions per face. Its own results already show that this protocol can decide the outcome: one VLM moves from chance to close to expert agreement when only the prompt changes. We keep the images, expert ratings and metric and change only how the answer is asked for and read: one yes/no question per category, scored by the probability of "yes". Scored from parsed text on the five categories experts agree on most, eleven open-weight VLMs average a quadratic-weighted $\kappa$ of 0.425 against individual experts, below the 0.468 at which two experts agree. Scored from yes-probabilities, the same models average 0.553, and all eleven agree with an individual expert better than a second expert does. The VLMs' mean is level with the benchmark's fine-tuned model (0.555), and three of them significantly exceed it without any training. Only one exceeds a stricter reference, the mean of three experts scored against the fourth (0.563). Verdicts that VLMs fail at graded facial affect ratings may therefore describe the readout more than the model. A fine-tuned model should have to beat a pretrained VLM read this way before it is called necessary, and the benchmark's own does not clearly do so.

articles.title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.20431v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in scientific research aims to improve agents' research capabilities through their own experimental experience. Scientific agent swarms can combine evidence and implementations from different research directions to guide their agents' subsequent experiments. However, poor experimental results can leave unclear whether to revise a hypothesis or its implementation, while overall program scores can hide components useful to other agents. To address these challenges, we introduce SwarmRSI, a framework that evolves scientific agent swarms for recursive self-improvement. We devise Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation to refine hypotheses and their implementations using experimental feedback from other agents. We also propose Complementary Swarm Recombination to reuse retained hypotheses and complementary program components across agents, allowing partial results to support new research. Recursive Swarm Evolution integrates both mechanisms into a feedback loop, using new experimental evidence to guide subsequent research. Experiments on OpenProblems, NatureBench and MLE-Bench Lite demonstrate SwarmRSI's state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. Further evaluations show that accumulated research experience improves performance on held-out tasks. Biologists also reproduce its programs for follow-up biological analyses.

articles.title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.21270v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. We instantiate an episode-level evaluation protocol as 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes: 40 hand-authored semantic seeds across four task classes, two surface parameterizations, and five controlled variants, scored on ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE under a pre-declared 5:1 missed-versus-unnecessary escalation cost. Reference actions are single-author study-policy labels, not clinician-adjudicated ground truth. Across five open-weight configurations (1.7B--9.7B), clean decision accuracy reaches 0.97, yet uncertainty-prompted models miss 32--97% of required escalations. The stronger 9.7B configuration narrows but does not remove the gap, falling from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict. Verbalized confidence is inconsistent (ECE 0.10--0.54; failure AUROC 0.48--0.77), and a development-tuned confidence-only policy yields no utility gain. A transparent workflow-aware controller improves 5:1 utility for every model and reduces missed escalations to 0.12--0.24, at specificity 0.83--0.93. However, a 30-concept lexical stress test reduces each rule detector's recall from 1.00 on trigger phrases to 0.00 on unseen paraphrases, limiting the controller claim to this benchmark. Seed-clustered statistics, ablations, cross-task transfer, raw outputs, and manifests are packaged for audit. The results motivate explicit workflow-state evaluation while showing that apparently effective routing controls need their own generalization tests.

articles.title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.28397v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.

articles.title: Finitely Verifiable Segmentation: Decidability for Every Tokenizer with a Finite-State Verifier
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.30168v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A segmentation policy assigns to each byte string at most one segmentation into tokens. Call it finitely verifiable when a finite automaton over marked strings, bytes paired with boundary bits, accepts exactly the policy's own segmentations. The automaton judges a proposed segmentation and need not compute one. From a supplied verifier the paper gives constructive decisions for four questions, whether a window certifies a token boundary, whether the boundary gap is bounded, whether a mask can keep generation from dead-ending, and whether two policies are equivalent. The last three specialize limitedness, co-accessibility and the equivalence of single-valued transducers. The first refines the synchronizing cut of code theory, and two more ask whether a certified cut, or the cuts of an inventory, let each piece scan alone. The class sits strictly between the online-scannable policies and those with regular domains, and online scannability is decidable in polynomial time through Choffrut's theorem. Markings are length-preserving, so the class is exactly the rational segmentation policies, a normal form rather than a restriction. The class is closed under four pipeline operations, composition over a labeled stage, restriction to a regular schema, splitting at character-class changes, and byte-fallback union of literal policies. Each composite inherits the six decisions, and certificates transfer between stages under four laws. Under rational, unifilar, almost surely stopping finite-state sources, each mass of the weighted section is an exact rational, and so is each rate where expected length is positive. Maximal-munch lexing, canonical byte-pair encoding and two-mode WordPiece instantiate the interface, and the munch library implements all six decisions. Every theorem carries an executable check, and every reported statistic is a program's own output.

articles.title: Beyond fabrication: Misattributed numbers in papers written by AI research agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.38691v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Verifying numerical claims in research written by AI agents is an important but challenging problem. Recent benchmarks show that many agent-written papers fail integrity checks, but such verdicts, often produced by a single LLM judge, identify failure without explaining its nature, and existing checks either test a paper for internal consistency or test whether a reported value appears somewhere in an agent's output. We re-analyze all 540 released judgments from a recent public benchmark of AI research agents (nine agents, fifteen open research problems) and manually label 256 numerical claims from 18 submissions. Failures concentrate on alignment between the paper and the underlying work rather than overt cheating, and about four in five unsupported claims correspond to values in the agent's own files that come from the wrong experiment, metric, or run. We introduce a deterministic claim-to-evidence checker that scores whether the surrounding context identifies the claimed result and calibrates each claim against numerical decoys. With its rules fixed before labeling, it certifies claims with over 90% precision against blinded annotators (78 of 85; Cohen's kappa = 0.89), while verifying only a subset of claims; most claims it cannot verify are nevertheless traceable, so failure to verify is not evidence of falsehood. An LLM verifier given the same evidence recovers more traceable claims but accepts about three times as many misattributed ones, so the two are best used together. Applied to 99 submissions, the checker reveals large differences in traceability across agents, and on 30 submissions a second judge configuration, with a different model and harness, orders the agents' vendor groups as the official judge does while passing twice as many papers. These findings motivate provenance-first auditing of AI-produced research.

articles.title: Efficient Agentic Audio-Visual Question Answering through Toolset Pruning and Modality Consolidation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.38960v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Fine-grained audio-visual question answering (AVQA) requires models to resolve complex cross-modal correspondences and temporally grounding from sparsely distributed evidence. Omni-modal agents, which autonomously orchestrate perception tools to actively collect evidence, achieve strong performance, but it remains unclear whether active perception from both audio and visual modalities depends on broad specialized toolsets, especially audio or visual modality-specific tools. Such systems may also introduce long execution trajectories and substantial inference cost. We investigate whether comparable performance can be retained with a compact workflow exposing only essential perceptual capabilities. Starting from the specialized-tool OmniAgent, we conduct staged controlled experiments that prune the toolset and progressively consolidate modality-specific tools into omni-modal tools, motivating a two-tool agent comprising only Omni-modal captioning and Omni-modal QA. Across three widely used AVQA benchmarks, our compact agent achieves comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent while reducing inference cost by around 70%.

articles.title: Leveraging Recourse and Size Bounds for OnlineKnapsack with Removable Items
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.40290v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In the online unweighted knapsack problem, items arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected immediately for a bounded-capacity knapsack, aiming to maximize the total size of accepted items. When decisions are irrevocable, no algorithm achieves a non-trivial competitive ratio. An essential relaxation that circumvents this impossibility is to allow previously accepted items to be removed from the knapsack (a.k.a. removal). In this work, we investigate possible further improvements on the competitive ratio with removal by bringing together two other previously proposed model extensions: knowledge of an upper bound on the item sizes (a.k.a. bound awareness) and ability to reinsert previously rejected items(a.k.a.recourse). Our contributions are twofold. First, we establish close upper and lower bounds on the competitive ratio under bound awareness, removal and recourse. We show that significant improvements on the best known competitive ratio are possible when the upper bound on the item sizes is not too restrictive and only few uses of recourse are available. Second, we introduce the notion of adaptive online algorithms which do not require to know any upper bound on the item sizes but still achieve performance guarantees comparable to the ones obtained under the bound awareness model.

articles.title: A Generalized Sparse Fuzzy Clustering Framework with Automated Cluster Cardinality Estimation Ability
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00159v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fuzzy clustering provides a robust framework for handling ambiguous and overlapping data boundaries, yet its traditional formulation generates entirely dense membership assignments that limit noise resilience and prevent estimating the true number of clusters, when it is unknown. To address these limitations, we introduce in this paper the Generalized Sparse Fuzzy Clustering (GSFC) framework, which incorporates a continuous sparsity penalty into the fuzzy objective function. Because closed-form solutions are precluded by the simultaneous presence of fuzzifier and sparsity exponents, we propose an efficient primal-dual bisection search coupled with specialized analytic pathways to rigorously enforce the partition constraint while organically driving trace memberships to exact zero. This mathematically enforced sparsity empowers the algorithm to autonomously estimate the true number of clusters by dynamically pruning redundant clusters, provided that it is initialized by a larger than the true number of clusters. Furthermore, we integrate a virtual noise sink to insulate outliers from the rest of the data points. The usage of the proposed framework is also extended to line segment detection. Extensive empirical evaluations across synthetic toy datasets, high-noise geometric stress tests, and real-world benchmarks (UCI wine dataset and hyperspectral images) demonstrate that GSFC effectively exceeds conventional fuzzy benchmarks while autonomously resolving cluster cardinality. Additionally, it significantly outperforms existing sparse possibilistic and probabilistic soft-clustering alternatives in line detection tasks.

articles.title: Learning to bid and bundle: a posterior-sampling agent for online retail
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00165v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An online retailer launching a perishable product bids for sponsored-search clicks, discounts a bundle with an always-stocked staple and displays its remaining stock, which raises willingness to pay. It knows neither how clicks respond to its bid nor how strong and dispersed its market is, and learns both over repeated seasons from data its own decisions censor: a zero bid reveals nothing about paid clicks, and choices follow only clicks. We design a posterior-sampling agent for it. Each period it draws a market from an exact posterior and posts the bid and discount of that market's exactly solved season plan, so every action is one a fully informed seller could take. In a simulated online florist it has the lowest regret averaged over markets. In weak markets it gives up 12% to 23% of one season's revenue over 500 seasons, four to seven times less than drawing once per season. A planner acting on point estimates can stop bidding and never learn that bidding pays. The agent escapes after about three seasons on average, against fifty with one draw per season. Where displayed scarcity keeps willingness to pay above the posted price, the discount needs no learning. Customers waiting for the discount to return to its recent level look like lost sales, so frequent waiting makes the agent underrate its market. One discount per season removes waiting at a cost of 5.9% of clairvoyant revenue in a weak market and none in a strong one.

articles.title: Early Stopping in Large Reasoning Models: A Survey and Empirical Audit of Efficiency and Reliability
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00166v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large reasoning models can improve accuracy by generating longer reasoning traces, but some of this computation may be unnecessary. Early-stopping methods aim to stop once enough reasoning is available to answer. Evaluating these methods requires accounting for the cost of deciding when to stop and the reliability of the resulting answer. We evaluate different methods across five reasoning models on mathematical and scientific reasoning, code generation, and factuality tasks by using a shared rollout replay protocol. We introduce Target-Integrated Token Efficiency (TITE) to measure efficiency relative to the oracle across accuracy targets. We also examine correctness at later exit positions, transfer across models and tasks, post-stop reasoning continuation, and retained justification quality. In our experiments, correctness can decrease at later positions beyond what the fitted decoding-noise model predicts. Reliability checks also reveal continued reasoning after forced termination and weaker supporting reasoning in some correct early-stopping outputs. The implementation can be found in https://github.com/hung20gg/audit-early-stopping.

articles.title: PatchScout: Thematic Web Data Collection via Information Foraging
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00169v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Researchers often need web corpora that are not answers to a single query, but reusable collections of documents spanning many decentralized sources. We refer to this problem as thematic web data collection: assembling semantically relevant documents that share a common theme but are scattered across heterogeneous and structurally disconnected regions of the web. Existing approaches, including traversal-based methods and LLM-driven web agents, are limited by local exploration or short-horizon stopping, preventing comprehensive collection. We formulate this task as a long-horizon information foraging problem over query-induced semantic patches, where the central challenge is deciding when to continue local exploitation and when to switch to new regions. We propose PatchScout, a multi-agent framework that instantiates a class of patch-switching policies to balance local exploitation and adaptive patch switching under a fixed budget. Experiments on four live-web topics show that PatchScout substantially improves yield and domain coverage over traversal-based and search-augmented reasoning agent baselines. In an applied social science setting with an incomplete prior collection, PatchScout discovers 102 previously unidentified entities, illustrating its ability to expand existing thematic datasets.

articles.title: Reimagining Text-to-SQL: A Survey of Large Language Model Architectures and Strategies
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00171v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-SQL systems translate natural language questions into executable SQL queries, democratizing access to relational data. Early approaches relied on handcrafted rules and template matching, while subsequent neural methods introduced encoder-decoder architectures, schema linking, and constrained decoding to handle increasingly complex queries. The emergence of large language models (LLMs), exemplified by systems such as ReFoRCE, Agentar-Scale-SQL, Snowflake's Arctic-Text2SQL-R1, and the modular XiYan-SQL framework, has dramatically advanced the field, pushing execution accuracy to new state-of-the-art levels on challenging benchmarks such as Spider, Spider 2.0, and BIRD. In parallel, modular frameworks decompose the task into sub-problems (schema retrieval, sketch-based generation, repair, and ranking), while agentic systems coordinate multiple specialized agents that communicate and dynamically allocate sub-tasks. This survey systematically reviews these LLM-driven approaches within a unified taxonomy of five paradigms (in-context learning, supervised and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, agentic and tool-augmented orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation, and reinforcement learning) and characterizes them by model granularity (monolithic vs. modular), level of supervision (zero-shot, fine-tuned, or reinforcement-based), and reasoning style (direct decoding vs. decomposed multi-step reasoning). We further analyze evaluation metrics, datasets, and open challenges, including domain generalization, efficiency, and real-world deployment, and we examine the role of the semantic layer in production systems. As LLMs increasingly access sensitive databases, we also discuss responsible AI practices. We survey over 100 papers and technical resources, focusing on work published between 2022 and 2026.

articles.title: AuroraWorld: Structured 4D World Modeling for Exo-to-Ego Video Generation in Robot Manipulation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00177v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Egocentric observations provide a robot-centric view of manipulation processes, capturing contact interactions and object-state changes that are important for visuomotor policy learning but difficult to observe from external cameras. However, collecting such data at scale remains expensive due to additional hardware requirements and platform-specific deployment costs. Synthesizing egocentric observations from large-scale exocentric manipulation videos provides a scalable alternative. However, existing methods struggle to synthesize physically consistent and policy-relevant egocentric videos under substantial viewpoint transformations, severe occlusions, complex object interactions, and inherently sparse observations from available exocentric viewpoints.

articles.title: Neurons Are All You Need
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00186v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: For decades, artificial neural networks have operated under the assumption that durable, learned capability resides exclusively in adaptive synaptic parameters, primarily due to the established neurobiology of synaptic connectivity. This design forces models to remain stateless during deployment, incurring well-known limitations such as catastrophic forgetting and expensive retraining. However, recent neurobiological research by Glanzman and colleagues, and others, shows that memories can be transferred between individual organisms in a synaptically independent manner. Inspired by this research, we sought to demonstrate memory transfer of persistent memory between AI model instances, leveraging a neurocentric version of memory. In this paper, we propose NURESA (Neural Unit with Retentive Self-Adaptive Architecture), a novel neural layer that eschews sole reliance on synaptic weight updating by introducing persistent intra-unit memory as a first-class, computational primitive. By structurally separating computation from persistent memory, NURESA enables autonomous memory accumulation and consolidation into transferable stores of memory registers. Experiments across MLP, GPT-2, and modern frontier models like Qwen2.5 demonstrate qualitatively new capability: zero-shot transfer of learned capability into a naive model instance without retraining or access to the original training data; this transfer is enabled by a sparse set of parameters in NURESA's memory register that the model selects on its own based on which neurons were most active. The memory transfer capability of NURESA also protects against domain loss when transformer models undergo learning via fine-tuning. Finally, the memory transfer process completes in approximately one minute even for transformer models with millions to billions of parameters, producing a transfer file orders of magnitude smaller than the original model.

articles.title: MemU-Bench: Benchmarking GUI Agents on Long-Horizon User Interactions
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00191v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing Graphical User Interface (GUI) benchmarks predominantly rely on precise and stateless user instructions. In everyday usage, however, instructions are often \emph{vague and history-dependent}: users omit the exact details of their past operations because they no longer remember them, leaving the agent to recover the missing context from long and noisy interaction histories. To bridge this evaluation gap, we introduce \textbf{MemU-Bench}, a mobile benchmark of \textbf{118 vague tasks} grounded in 29 long-horizon user trajectories, where agents must distill raw interaction streams into memory and retrieve the missing context on demand, with task outcomes verified against serialized application databases. Alongside Success Rate, we incorporate Interaction Efficiency (IE) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) to expose agents that succeed by exhaustively searching across different applications rather than by \emph{genuinely recalling} the history. Evaluations show that without user history, state-of-the-art systems struggle under such ambiguity: the best-performing Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves an SPL of only 16.4\%, and end-to-end GUI agents fall below 5\%. To address this, we further propose \textbf{AppMem}, a training-free framework that distills user history into a \emph{structured, app-centric} memory bank, tracks interrupted intents across application switches, and selectively retrieves relevant memories via target-app inference. AppMem raises the SPL of GPT-5.5 from 15.7\% to 66.9\% (\textbf{+51.2\%}), outperforms a naive summary baseline by 9.3\%, and delivers consistent gains across evaluated backbones.

articles.title: From Cross-Section to Cross-Omics: Conditional Cell Nucleus Image Editing in Spatial Transcriptomics
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00226v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) platforms simultaneously measure gene expression and capture cell nucleus images at single-cell resolution. A fundamental property of tissue preparation introduces a confounding relationship between the two measurement modalities: sectioning a three-dimensional tissue into a thin slice produces a two-dimensional cross-section whose area depends on the cutting angle. Larger cross-sections expose more cytoplasm, yielding higher mRNA counts, while pathomics features such as nuclear area are measured directly from the same 2D boundary. This sectioning geometry creates an apparent correlation between gene expression and pathomics that reflects the measurement process rather than independent biology. Existing gene-to-image methods generate cell images from gene features but do not support condition-driven editing of existing images across both omics layers. We apply the Manifold-Aware Diffusion (MAD) framework to this dual-omics editing setting, enabling targeted modification of one feature group while preserving the other. Evaluated on podocyte cells from CosMx SMI kidney tissue, MAD achieves MAE=0.6636 and FID=25.19 for pathomics editing, outperforming all compared baselines. A controlled simulation study further confirms that the VAE component in MAD better preserves cross-group independence than CCDM (MAD without VAE).

articles.title: RE-SciVQA: Improving Scientific VQA With Context-Relevant Retrieval and Lightweight MLLM Adaptation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00242v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A deep understanding of scientific literature often relies on interpreting figures that contain key information beyond the main text. Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract insights from these figures can significantly accelerate knowledge discovery. Existing works on Scientific Visual Question Answering rely on resource-intensive training pipelines that are often inaccessible and require large computational resources. Instead of designing complex architectures, we propose RE- SciVQA, which focuses on improving the quality of retrieved context and fine-tuning small LLMs with parameter-efficient LoRA training. Using a simple query expansion step, relevant section headers are appended to the original question to improve the retrieval coverage. In addition, a simple adjustment of similarity scores is applied using figure references and caption alignment. On the SciVQA benchmark, RE-SciVQA achieves a ROUGE-1 F1 score of 73.9%, outperforming chart-focused models such as UniChart (14.7%), ChartGemma (6.9%), and Matcha-ChartQA (6.3%). Our relevance-enhanced RAG setup also improves the exact match by 11.9% and the fuzzy match by 29.5% compared with a standard RAG baseline, resulting in an overall gain of 14.3%. We also examine closed-ended infinite visual questions, a category in which chart-understanding models often struggle. Our experiments show that using plot digitization instead of synthetic captions leads to an 18.5% improvement for this question type.

articles.title: OmniPiano: Diverse Dexterous Piano-Playing Challenges for Standard, Robust, Safe, and Multi-Agent RL
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00243v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dexterous robotic manipulation remains a major challenge in robotics, exemplified by piano playing, which requires coordinated control of fingers and provides a demanding testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). Although previous work established a benchmark for robotic piano playing, it is restricted to two hands and does not support unified evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce OmniPiano, a benchmark that provides one to up to five Shadow Hands and supports standard, robust, safe, and multi-agent RL within a shared piano-playing task family. OmniPiano is developed for scalable and diverse piano-playing tasks with configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation settings. Particularly, to facilitate usability and extendability, OmniPiano adopts a highly modular design and provides comprehensive tasks to support RL study of task performance, robustness, safety, and cooperation in dexterous control. With at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, OmniPiano further incorporates LLM-based agents to broaden the evaluation scope and reveal new insights. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art RL algorithms and frontier LLM-based agents still struggle on challenging piano-playing tasks, even under standard RL settings, highlighting substantial room for improvement in dexterous control. The code, dataset, tutorial, and demo are available at https://sail-research-lab.github.io/omnipiano/.

articles.title: Taurus: LLM-in-the-Loop CT Annotation Matches Coding Agents at Half the Cost
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00247v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dense labels of the aorta in CT are slow to draw, and the public aortic CT datasets that could stand in for them each label different structures under their own conventions. Large language model (LLM) agents can now write code and read images. We asked whether such a model labels these scans better as a free-form agent that writes its own segmentation code, or inside a harness, where an automated pass labels the scan and the model reviews the result. We built a harness, Taurus, and compared it with free-form agents by blind label recovery: we withheld the human labels of six public datasets (939 volumes) and scored every approach against each dataset's own classes.
