In this paper, our key insight is that modern Large Language Models (LLMs) undergo alignment (including fine-tuning and preference tuning), leaving a measurable distributional imprint. We theoretically derive this imprint by abstracting the alignment process as a sequence of constrained optimization steps, showing that the log-likelihood ratio can naturally decompose into implicit instructional biases and preference rewards. We refer to this quantity as the Alignment Imprint. Furthermore, to mitigate the instability in high-entropy regions, we introduce Log-likelihood Alignment Preference Discrepancy (LAPD), a standardized information-weighted statistic based on alignment imprint. We provide statistical guarantee that alignment-based statistics dominate Fast-DetectGPT in performance. We also theoretically show that LAPD strictly improves the unweighted alignment scores when the aligned and base models are close in distribution. Extensive experiments show that LAPD achieves an improvement 45.82% relative to the strongest existing baselines, yielding large and consistent gains across all settings.

articles.title: ZenBrain: A Neuroscience-Inspired 7-Layer Memory Architecture for Autonomous AI Systems
articles.summary:
arXiv:2604.23878v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: ZenBrain is a seven-layer, neuroscience-derived architecture for agent memory in LLM agents. An open library holds the seven layers, a MemoryCoordinator and nine foundational algorithms; six Predictive Memory Architecture components run in a private production system. In the open library at version 0.5.1, decay acts only on working memory and nothing is replayed.
  Ablating one component at a time exposes an effect we call cooperative masking. The ablation runs in a simulation harness that switches fifteen components as stand-ins at simulated values, not as production code. Under moderate load, fourteen of the fifteen ablations look costless. Raising decay, the horizon, the corpus and the queries, with no change to the components, moves ten of the fifteen in the same direction on all ten seeds - nine losses (Delta-Q down to -93.7%) and one gain. With ten seeds this is the one p-value the normal approximation of the Wilcoxon test can reach (5.06e-3), and it does not pass the Bonferroni-corrected level for fifteen contrasts (3.33e-3).
  On LongMemEval_S (500 questions), the evaluated ZenBrain arm - a Python port of a scoring class from our test harness, not the seven-layer system - answers 47.7% of the questions correctly under a binary judge (95% interval [43.3, 52.1]). With the compared systems' adapters repaired, Letta reaches 48.4% and Mem0 47.2%. ZenBrain reaches 91.3% of a full-context baseline's accuracy with 1/109.7 of its input tokens in the answer step; building the memory is not counted. Of nine head-to-head comparisons of the retrieved context (3 competitors x 3 LLM judges), three hold at Bonferroni-corrected significance, all against A-Mem, and the remaining six show no significant difference.
  On LoCoMo, the routing results of version 8 came from placeholder embeddings; with text-embedding-3-small, the flat variant (F1 0.059) lies above the full system (0.058).

articles.title: The Circuit Basis of Metacognitive Failure in Language Models: Interference and Hallucination
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.05686v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Language models often answer with high confidence, as measured by output entropy, even when they are wrong. We study two situations that lead to such errors, knowledge conflict, where the context contradicts a fact stored in the weights and the two sources interfere, and missing knowledge, where the fact was never learned and the model hallucinates. To control what the model knows, we fine-tune it on synthetic facts that map arbitrary entity identifiers to random codes, installed through LoRA adapters on the MLP, query-key (QK), or value-output (VO) components of the transformer. Our analysis suggests that MLP is the main substrate for storing facts in basins, regions where a fact's representations converge, while QK steers generation toward a basin or the context, and VO writes the retrieved content into the residual stream. Under knowledge conflict, the form of interference depends on how the fact is learned. A fact learned from a single phrasing yields to the context, with each adapter leaving an error pattern consistent with its circuit role. A fact learned from many phrasings overrides the context, and under contradiction the answer starts on the stored code and drifts away from it. Under missing knowledge, the hidden state reaches no basin, yet every adapter placement produces confident hallucinations, VO most of all. In both situations, output entropy reflects how sharply the model commits rather than whether the answer is correct, even though the model's representations still separate correct answers from errors. Across 12 pretrained models, the hallucination rate falls with scale, but a growing fraction of the remaining hallucinations are confident. In the models we study, the gap between confidence and correctness does not close with scale, and flagging these errors requires confidence that reflects where the answer comes from, rather than how sharply the model commits to it.

articles.title: Switchcraft: AI Model Router for Agentic Tool Calling
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.07112v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Agentic AI systems that invoke external tools are powerful but costly, leading developers to default to large models and overspend inference budgets. Existing model routers target chat responses or end-task success, not the correctness of the individual tool calls on which agent tasks depend; we present Switchcraft, the first (to the best of our knowledge) model router optimized for strict tool-call correctness in agentic workloads. We construct an evaluation framework on six function-calling benchmarks, holding one out entirely, and fine-tune a calibrated DistilBERT-based classifier, deployed inline under a latency budget, to select the lowest-cost model subject to correctness or abstain when none is likely to answer correctly. Switchcraft reaches 78.3% answer accuracy (86.4% when correct abstentions are credited) at 59% lower cost than the best individual model (75.6%), saving over $3,800 per million queries, and outperforms kNN, MIRT, heuristic, and random routers. On the held-out benchmark, it matches or exceeds every individual model at 5--7X lower cost than the strongest ones. We find two counter-intuitive results: larger models do not consistently outperform smaller ones on tool-use tasks, and nominally cheaper models can incur higher total cost due to token-intensive output.

articles.title: Can You Break RLVER? Probing Adversarial Robustness of RL-Trained Empathetic Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.07138v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable emotion rewards (RLVER) yields strong empathetic language models, but is evaluated with cooperative, honest simulated users. Real users gaslight, escalate, and demand unconditional validation. We introduce the Adversarial Empathy Benchmark (AEB), six adversarial trajectory types whose discriminative rewards penalize formulaic comfort, and the Emotional Consistency Score (ECS), which separates whether a model \emph{improves} the user's emotional state from whether that state stays legible in the transcript. Across eight scenario-matched conditions (480 dialogues; two RLVER and two Qwen2.5 base models, with and without thinking), RLVER-PPO-Think outperforms its untuned same-scale baseline (FS $0.979$ vs.\ $0.761$, $p<10^{-12}$) with no dialogue collapses and 53\% higher hidden-intention detection; the gain is not explained by response length. Yet under an independent cross-family judge (Gemma-3-4b-it), ECS is indistinguishable between the two ($p=0.43$). We call this an outcome--legibility dissociation: RLVER improves emotional outcomes without making the user's state more legible. We do not claim ECS measures internal understanding.

articles.title: M$^3$: Reframing Training Measures for Discretized Physical Simulations
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.08843v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Neural surrogate models for physical simulations are trained on discretized samples of continuous domains, where the induced empirical measure leads to uneven supervision, biasing optimization and causing spatial inconsistencies in physical fidelity. To mitigate this measure-induced bias, we propose M$^3$ (Multi-scale Morton Measure), a scalable framework that balances training measures by partitioning space according to physical variation and allocating supervision across multiple scales. Applied to three industrial-scale datasets with diverse discretizations, M$^3$ consistently improves predictions in the continuous physical domain, achieving up to 4.7$\times$ lower error in large-scale volumetric cases. These gains persist under aggressive subsampling (160M $\rightarrow$ 16M $\rightarrow$ 1.6M points), where M$^3$-trained models outperform those trained on higher-resolution data, reducing physics-weighted relative $L_2$ error by 3--4$\times$ and the corresponding MSE by up to 13$\times$. These results highlight data distribution as a key factor in operator learning and position M$^3$ as a scalable, data-efficient approach for physically consistent modeling. Code is available at https://github.com/PhysDataRefine/M3.

articles.title: Teacher-Aware Evolution of Heuristic Programs from Learned Optimization Policies
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.10634v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM-based automatic heuristic design has shown promise for generating executable heuristics for combinatorial optimization, but existing methods mainly rely on delayed endpoint performance. We propose a \emph{teacher-aware evolutionary framework} that uses independently trained learned optimization policies as behavioral teachers. Instead of deploying or imitating the teacher, our method queries it on states visited by candidate heuristic programs and uses its action preferences as local feedback for evolution. The resulting search discovers static executable heuristics guided by both task performance and teacher-derived behavioral signals. Experiments on scheduling, routing, and graph optimization benchmarks show that our method improves over performance-driven LLM heuristic evolution baselines while requiring no neural inference at deployment. These results suggest that learned optimization policies can be repurposed as behavioral feedback sources for automatic heuristic discovery.

articles.title: Automated Reformulation of Robust Optimization via Memory-Augmented Large Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.11813v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Robust optimization (RO) provides a principled framework for decision-making under uncertainty, but its practical use is often limited by the need to manually reformulate uncertain optimization models into tractable deterministic counterparts. Recent large language models (LLMs) have been shown promising for automating optimization formulation, yet RO reformulation remains challenging because it requires precise multi-step reasoning and mathematically consistent transformations. To facilitate systematic evaluation of LLM-based reformulation, for which no dedicated benchmark currently exists, we develop AutoRO-Bench, a benchmark featuring an automated data generation pipeline for the core RO reformulation task and a curated dataset for the RO application task. To address the reformulation challenge, we propose Automated Reformulation with Experience Memory (AutoREM), a tuning-free memory-augmented framework that autonomously builds a structured textual experience memory by reflecting on past failed trajectories through a tailored offline adaptation procedure. AutoREM requires neither domain-specific expert knowledge nor parameter updates, and the resulting memory readily transfers across different base LLMs. Experimental results show that AutoREM consistently improves the accuracy and efficiency of RO reformulation across in-distribution datasets, out-of-distribution datasets, and diverse base LLMs.

articles.title: Isomorphism Is Not Enough: An Agentic Audit of Verified Code Generation in Lean
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.23772v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Agentic systems have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for automated theorem proving in formal mathematics. To assess how far these capabilities extend to program verification and how reliably existing benchmarks can measure them, we audit CLEVER, a Lean 4 benchmark for verifiable code generation, using three independent agentic stacks based on Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, and Kimi K2.5. Our audit finds arguably erroneous reference specifications in 80 of 161 entries, each accepted by the benchmark's authors, distills a taxonomy of benchmark errors, and exposes structural limitations of isomorphism-based scoring, whose signal breaks down when generated and reference specifications formalize different yet defensible readings. In the process, the stacks generate arguably valid specifications for up to 98.8% of entries, certify implementations against sound reference specifications for up to 92.3%, and reach up to 96.2% end-to-end success over entries with sound premises, suggesting that CLEVER no longer stresses modern agentic provers as much as its design intended. Looking ahead, we translate our findings into recommendations for future work, with our error analysis doubling as a repair list for CLEVER and a heuristic checklist for the next generation of benchmarks.

articles.title: When Does Multi-Agent RL Improve LLM Workflows? Workflow, Scale, and Policy-Sharing Tradeoffs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.24202v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Outcome-reward RL can train every role of a multi-agent LLM workflow. Its benefit is hard to predict because the reward assigns no credit to individual roles and a shared policy trades pooled data against specialization. We ask when this training improves a workflow over its base model and single-agent RL, and what each role learns. We train three workflows (Eval-Opt, Voting, Orch-Workers) with GRPO on math and code at three Qwen3 scales, with one policy for all roles (Shared-Policy, SP) or one per role type (Isolated-Policy, IP). Every workflow gains by adapting to its structure; this does not make a role better than training it alone. Single-agent RL in the same structure matches or beats trained Voting and Orch-Workers, and within the grid only Eval-Opt under IP exceeds it. Eval-Opt's evaluator learns when to retry and its generator learns to complete the retried attempts, a joint strategy that a single policy trained alone does not acquire. Under SP, per-output token averaging sets each role's gradient share, a hidden hyperparameter absent from single-agent RL, and the solving roles learn slowly; reweighting it gives SP the speed and peak of IP, and its decline. Under IP, a parallel role, whose instances share one adapter, takes one optimizer step per instance per training step and can drift after the peak as its entropy rises and accuracy declines. Merging those steps delays the decline.
  Our code is at: https://github.com/XHMY/marl-llm-workflows

articles.title: Anchor: Preventing Artifact Drift for Reliable Agent Verification
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.26321v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reliable evaluation of long-horizon agents requires verifiers that match what the task actually asks. Verifiable rewards have driven progress in domains like math and coding, yet building similarly reliable environments for open-ended enterprise workflows repeatedly struggles to balance realism, verifiability, and scale. This creates a validity problem we call artifact drift: when instructions, environments, oracles, and verifiers are created separately, they frequently fail to agree on what a task requires, resulting in environments that are unsolvable, reward-hackable, or inconsistent. We introduce Anchor, a benchmark-construction pipeline that formalizes domain expert specifications of business workflows into constrained optimization programs. From a single parametric specification, the pipeline jointly produces a natural-language instruction, environment configuration, solver-certified ground-truth solution, and state-based verifier. With this pipeline, altering parameters yields new tasks with controlled difficulty and known optimal solutions, producing harness-agnostic environments whose rewards depend solely on end-state business correctness. We apply Anchor to produce ERP-Bench: a benchmark of 300 long-horizon tasks spanning procurement and manufacturing workflows in a production-grade ERP system. Our pipeline organizes tasks into diverse families with calibrated difficulty profiles, and allows generated environments to evaluate coding, browser, and computer-use agents using a shared verifier. Across these harnesses, we find that frontier models follow all rules and instructions in 25.9% of trials and reach fully optimal decisions in only 17.4% of trials. Overall, Anchor and ERP-Bench offer a concrete recipe for building auditable evaluation environments whose verifiers remain aligned with the economically valuable tasks they are intended to score.

articles.title: SkillDAG: Self-Evolving Typed Skill Graphs for LLM Skill Selection at Scale
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.03056v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large skill libraries are now standard equipment for LLM agents, and which subset reaches the prompt decides what the agent can do. Enumeration and top-$K$ embedding retrieval both treat skills as independent documents, assuming relevance is a property of one skill at a time. It is not: skills depend on, conflict with, specialize, and duplicate one another, so the closest match to a task can name it while omitting a prerequisite it needs. Graph retrieval encodes these relations but spends them in a fixed pipeline, handing the agent an opaque bundle. We present SkillDAG, which exposes a typed skill graph to the LLM as an agent-callable interface rather than consuming it for the agent: search returns vector matches, typed-edge neighbors, and conflict signals, and a propose-then-commit protocol lets it register execution-backed edges as it works. Across two benchmarks and three model families, SkillDAG outperforms full-library prompting, vector retrieval, and Graph-of-Skills, gaining +14.3 points of ALFWorld success and tying only at ceiling; its ranking holds flat across a $10\times$ pool expansion that degrades the fixed pipeline. Inter-skill structure, these results suggest, is worth more to an agent that can query and revise it than to a retriever that consumes it.

articles.title: MedCUA-Bench: A Screenshot-Only Benchmark for Clinical Computer-Use Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.03203v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Computer-use agents could automate repetitive screen-based clinical work, but their reliability in medical graphical user interfaces remains largely unvalidated. Existing benchmarks focus on general web or desktop tasks and underrepresent medical software, which requires domain knowledge, exhibits markedly different UI design from mainstream applications, lacks public testing environments, and demands safety validation beyond task completion. We introduce MedCUA-Bench, an interactive benchmark for clinical computer-use agents. It covers 18 clinical scenarios across 10 medical domains, reconstructed from real product manuals and open-source medical systems to capture authentic clinical interfaces while avoiding licensing and privacy constraints. Each task ships with paired intent- and step-level goals to disentangle clinical reasoning from UI execution, and is evaluated by a deterministic checker over task completion and five clinical safety dimensions. Across 23 agents, the best closed-source model reaches 54.2% strict success, while all models remain below 9% on the real OpenEMR. Open-source agents average only 2.5%, with the best reaching 16.2%. MedCUA-Bench exposes the gap between current agents and reliable clinical software use, providing a reproducible testbed for future research.

articles.title: Can Test-Time Reconstruction Close the Loop on Latent Reasoning?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.06252v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent work moves intermediate reasoning from natural-language traces into latent or cache-level representations to reduce token overhead and avoid a discrete communication bottleneck. However, this shift also removes a key advantage of textual reasoning: intermediate states are no longer inspectable, making it difficult to determine whether a latent state still preserves the constraints of the original query. As a result, latent reasoning typically operates in an open loop, where a latent state is produced and consumed without an input-anchored fidelity check. We propose ReLAT (Reconstruction-Guided Latent Reasoning At Test Time), a self-supervised test-time training method that closes this loop using the query itself as the reference. Our key observation is that if a latent state faithfully represents a query, the query should be recoverable from it; if the query cannot be recovered, the latent state has lost task-relevant information. ReLAT operationalizes this principle by constructing a differentiable Question -> Latent Thought -> Question cycle and optimizing query reconstruction loss through the latent thought before answer generation. This anchors opaque latent computation to the problem specification it is supposed to represent. Across mathematical reasoning, knowledge QA, and code generation benchmarks on the Qwen family, ReLAT consistently improves over single-model inference, text-based collaboration, open-loop latent collaboration, and alternative test-time training objectives. On Qwen3-8B, ReLAT raises AIME 2024 accuracy from 56.7% to 73.3%, a 16.6-point gain over the strongest open-loop latent baseline.

articles.title: Beyond Safe Data: Pretraining-Stage Alignment with Regular Safety Reflection
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.19168v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: To achieve deeper safety alignment for large language models (LLMs), recent efforts have studied how to push safety interventions earlier into the pretraining stage, primarily by filtering unsafe data or rewriting it into safer forms. We argue that pretraining-stage alignment should go beyond making the data safe: LLMs may generalize unsafe behaviors from seemingly benign pretraining data. To this end, we propose Safety Reflection Pretraining, a pretraining-stage alignment method which regularly inserts short safety reflections between sentences in pretraining corpora. This integrates self-monitoring directly into language modeling, establishing a foundational capability that is subsequently reinforced by compatible post-training. Our experiments with 1.7B models pretrained on FineWeb-Edu show that Safety Reflection Pretraining improves safety classification accuracy and substantially reduces the success rates of inference-stage and fine-tuning attacks. Complementary to our real-world experiments, we also introduce a fully controlled synthetic environment, MedSafetyWorld, with a clear definition of safety and a reasoning structure under which we find that models can easily generalize unsafe behaviors from safe data. Ablations in MedSafetyWorld further demonstrate a clear advantage of Safety Reflection Pretraining over data filtering and rewriting in preventing models from acting on unsafe behaviors. Taken together, our findings suggest that pretraining alignment should not only make the training data safe, but also shape the behaviors that models are likely to acquire from safe data.

articles.title: Harnessing Agent Skills: Architectural Patterns and a Reference Architecture for Skill-Mediated LLM Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.20631v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: CONTEXT: Agent skills package reusable behavioural guidance and resources that large language model agents load or apply during a run. Within the agent harness, agent skill harnessing comprises connected architectural responsibilities that govern which skills enter a run, which actions they can cause, and how their use is recorded and informs revision. OBJECTIVES: We identify architectural patterns for agent skill harnessing and organise their responsibilities into a reference architecture that makes these connections explicit. METHODS: A multivocal literature review covered 36 practitioner systems and 51 academic papers; we consolidated practices into patterns and derived the reference architecture from patterns, source evidence, and architectural reasoning. We evaluated the reference architecture by mapping eight systems and applying it in Deep Agents and Hermes Agent. RESULTS: Ten patterns cover skill supply and activation, skill declarations and execution authority, verification and recording of skill use, and run evidence feeding repair and governed revision. The reference architecture organises their responsibilities into four layers (Supply Chain, Mediation, Execution Control, Evidence & Feedback) and two cross-cutting substrates, separating permission determination from enforcement and routing persistent revisions through acceptance. Mapping eight systems showed the first three layers broadly realised and 14 of 15 partial or unestablished ratings in Evidence \& Feedback. Applying the architecture in Deep Agents and Hermes Agent turned requirements into checks that exposed a shell route outside the file-tool rules and a preview--apply mismatch. CONCLUSION: The patterns and reference architecture support comparing implementations and turning requirements into responsibility allocations and checks.

articles.title: OpenFinGym: A Verifiable Multi-Task Gym Environment for Evaluating Quant Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.26350v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Although large language model agents are increasingly applied to quantitative-finance workflows, their evaluation remains fragmented across isolated tasks, while the financial relevance of benchmark tasks is often overlooked. Yet financial workflows are inherently multi-stage, spanning interdependent tasks such as forecasting, strategy construction, risk management, and trading. Existing platforms typically focus on a single task, and can therefore overstate agent competence and fail to reveal weaknesses in generalization, real-market interaction, and financially meaningful decision-making. We introduce OpenFinGym, a unified gym environment for quantitative-finance agent development that covers forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection under a single execution and verification interface. OpenFinGym additionally provides an automated task-construction pipeline that turns quantitative finance publications into executable task packages; a containerised runtime with a host-side verifier service that supports scalable agent rollouts and prevents runtime train-test leakage; a paper trading engine with a low-latency data-stream design; deferred-resolution support for long-horizon and event-market forecasts; and integration for SFT and RL post-training.

articles.title: Be Faithful When Response: Returning Fluent and Grounded Answers for Vision-Language Models Reinforcement Learning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.29984v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is an important paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs). However, directly applying RL to rollout multimodal reasoning can lead to instability, due to the exploitation of language priors, the neglect of visual evidence, and the generation of reasoning traces that are fluent yet not visually grounded. The question arises: Can initially steer the policy toward visually faithful reasoning regime before applying reinforcement learning? To this end, we propose a Faithful Warm-Start (FWS) strategy that first curates samples with explicit vision-language causal relationships from six general VQA benchmarks to construct the FaithfulQA dataset, where each of the image-question pairs gains a certain degree of visual observations, question requirements, commonsense knowledge, domain knowledge, and the final answer. Subsequently, a VLM-based judge is employed to further purify the dataset, ensuring strong causal consistency and visual faithfulness. This warm-start stage equips the model with the capability to understand causally grounded vision-language patterns before subsequent RL optimization under sparse answer-level rewards. Experimental results show that such faithful supervision improves answer accuracy, stabilizes RL training, and reduces visually unsupported reasoning.

articles.title: GRATE: Temporal Extensions for Inductive KG Foundation Models via Gated Rotary Attention
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.10197v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Knowledge graph foundation models such as Ultra and Trix achieve strong inductive transfer by learning relation-graph representations that generalise to unseen entities and relations. Extending this transferability to temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) remains challenging: existing temporal models tie their parameters to dataset-specific entities, relations, or timestamps and are not designed to transfer to TKGs with disjoint vocabularies. We propose GRATE (Gated Rotary Attention for Temporal Encoding), an entity-side message function that adds no learnable parameters and encodes time through relative time differences by rotating each edge message according to its time gap to the query and applying a query-conditioned gate to select temporally relevant signals. GRATE integrates into NBFNet-style KG foundation models while preserving structural transferability. Existing TKG benchmarks evaluate within shared train/test vocabularies and cannot directly test cross-dataset temporal transfer; we therefore construct GDELTIndT and WIKIIndT, inductive transfer benchmark suites with disjoint entities, relations, and timestamps spanning both interpolation and extrapolation. Across these benchmarks and held-out forecasting datasets, a single jointly pretrained GRATE checkpoint improves over the static base model in most settings.

articles.title: HierFlow: Hierarchical Coupled Dual-Space Search for Automatic Agentic Workflow Generation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2607.21609v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Although structured workflows empower Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex problems, automating their creation is severely hindered by a vast combinatorial search space, frequently resulting in inflexible and resource-heavy offline training dependencies. To address this, we conceptualize workflow generation as an intertwined topology-and-execution search paradigm, where the broader topological layer dictates subtask boundaries and lower-level execution outcomes actively reshape the topology itself. Building on this foundation, we introduce HierFlow, a training-free, test-time hierarchical search architecture that automates agentic workflow design by merging feedback-guided topology adjustments with a fast, MCTS-inspired tree search for sub-workflow optimization. HierFlow maximizes efficiency through an intelligent gating module that selectively triggers execution-level searches based on contextual necessity, a mechanism we further support with an in-depth analysis detailing how varying degrees of cross-task coupling impact the effectiveness of hierarchical splitting. Comprehensive testing across question answering, mathematical reasoning, and code generation benchmarks confirms that HierFlow consistently outperforms strong baselines, delivering an optimal balance of high-quality results and computational efficiency without any additional training overhead.

articles.title: Modeling Social Dynamics with an LLM-Enabled Agent Based Network-Dynamic (LAND) Model
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.00929v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Social dynamics encode the process in which individual network and discourse interactions aggregate into collective influence, narrative dominance and coordinate behavior. This paper uses the the GhostField architecture, a hybrid LLM-Enabled Agent Based Network-Dynamic (LAND) model as a social simulation framework to build the AuraSight scenario. In the AuraSight scenario, 314,244 heterogeneous cyber social agents and human actors exchange 529,327 messages over 30 days surrounding a fictional international song-writing contest. We methodologically examine emergent social dynamics across four analytical layers: ego-network topology, semantic network evolution, coordination dynamics and influence dynamics. Our results show how generated social simulations do also produce social dynamics, and how the dynamics of coordination and influence emerge not from individual agents but from the recursive interaction between network topology and narrative exchange.

articles.title: Solver-Aware Decompositions for Programming-by-Example: When Dividing Requires Knowing How to Conquer
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.03461v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Decomposition-based Programming-by-Example splits a task into subtasks: a decomposer predicts intermediate subgoals, and a learned synthesizer generates a program for each subgoal. Execution-decomposition approaches train the decomposer to imitate ground-truth (GT) subgoals and thereby treat decomposition quality as a property of the task alone. A learned synthesizer, however, has its own inductive biases, and GT subgoals reflect how the annotator factorized the task, not what this synthesizer can solve. A decomposer that imitates them can therefore propose subgoals that are logically valid but intractable for the synthesizer. Motivated by this observation, we propose Solver-Aware Decompositions (SAD), which keeps supervised training on GT subgoals as a structural scaffold and additionally trains the decomposer online with self-critical policy gradients against a frozen synthesizer. Each sampled subgoal is rewarded with the negative cross-entropy of the synthesizer on the target program, a continuous signal of how difficult the subtask is for this synthesizer. Our experiments show an accuracy paradox: with the synthesizer fixed, a GT-supervised decomposer agrees more often with the GT subgoals, yet its subgoals lead to lower synthesis accuracy, although the synthesizer was trained on the same GT data. On two list-processing domains, SAD improves synthesis and task accuracy over the GT-supervised decomposer, both in-distribution and under length generalization; the same holds under zero-shot transfer to an external benchmark and for a fine-tuned language model. Even an oracle that receives the GT subgoals at inference time, with the same synthesizer and search, fails on tasks that SAD solves, and fewer than 2% of SAD's solutions to these tasks match the GT program. Decomposition quality is therefore not a property of the task: it depends on the synthesizer that executes the subgoals.

articles.title: A/B Agent: A Self-Evolving Agent for Strategy Iteration in Industrial A/B Testing
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.04625v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Industrial recommendation strategy iteration heavily relies on large-scale A/B experimentation. Traditional tuning requires experts to repeatedly design strategies, configure experiments, analyze results, and adjust parameters, making the process labor-intensive and time-consuming. Meanwhile, valuable knowledge from historical experiments is often fragmented, making systematic reuse difficult through manual expert effort alone. Existing RAG agents partially alleviate this burden by retrieving prior strategies, but typically organize experience in a flat manner, overlooking the hierarchical relationships among business scenarios, recommendation stages, optimization objectives, and experimental contexts. This often results in mismatched retrieval and limited cross-scenario transfer, while preventing agents from continuously refining strategies and parameters through sequential A/B feedback. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{\ourname}, a closed-loop A/B agent for industrial recommendation strategy optimization. The framework comprises three tightly coupled core components: \textit{Historical Strategy Knowledge Organization}, \textit{Autonomous Target-Aware Strategy Generation}, and \textit{Experiment-Guided Strategy Self-Evolution}. It organizes historical strategies into a hierarchical experience tree, retrieves transferable evidence through multi-path Tree-RAG to generate executable strategies, and continuously analyzes online A/B feedback to guide autonomous tuning and update the experience tree for self-evolution. Extensive offline and online evaluations demonstrate its effectiveness, including a \textbf{4.829%} improvement in GMV in a real-world short-video e-commerce recommendation system while maintaining positive gains across all guardrail metrics.

articles.title: Sanyu Studio: A Multi-Agent System for Art-Historical Narrative Construction
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.18677v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Amid concerns that generative AI may standardize art interpretation, this paper examines whether LLM-based interaction can support plural art-historical narrative construction. We present Sanyu Studio, a multi-agent dialogue system that models 321 Sanyu oil paintings as agents with fact, interpretation, organization, and memory-filtering mechanisms. Based on a seven-day workshop with eight art-university participants, the study shows that user prompts, evidence organization, and cognitive tendencies shaped divergent yet coherent versions of digital Sanyu. The findings suggest that, under conditions of limited historical evidence, AI can amplify human agency and offer public audiences an interactive entry point into art-historical interpretation.

articles.title: STAGE: Stateful Translation to Agentic Graph Execution with Policy-Scoped Context and Deterministic Control
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.22538v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Enterprise agents are expected to deliver correct and consistent outcomes while executing complex procedures, adhering to governing policies, and operating within practical resource budgets. We present \textsc{Stage}, an integrated execution framework combining typed task nodes, shared execution memory, document tools, and deterministic orchestration. We evaluate \textsc{Stage} on SOP-Bench Referral Abuse, the Retail and Telecom domains of $\tau^2$-bench, and two proprietary banking workflows, Smart Dispute and Paystub Fraud Detection. Using the same underlying model in each comparison, \textsc{Stage} improves single-run success and repeated-run reliability over the baseline in all 18 benchmark--model pairs. Success across all three runs (\(\mathrm{Pass}^{3}\)) increases by 7.5--66.0 percentage points. Fixed-graph ablations demonstrate the contributions of localized policy context and coordinator-owned routing. Further analysis of Smart Dispute shows improved coverage of required operations across procedure lengths. These findings show that integrating local reasoning, persistent state, and procedural control can improve reliable enterprise workflow completion without changing the underlying model.

articles.title: Reinforcement Learning-Guided Evolutionary Policy Optimization for Preference-Adjustable Heterogeneous Agile Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.24470v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Heterogeneous agile Earth observation satellite (AEOS) scheduling requires task selection, satellite assignment, and observation sequencing under satellite-dependent visibility windows, attitude maneuvering requirements, energy consumption, and onboard storage constraints. Since satellites differ in orbital access, maneuvering capability, and payload resources, the same task may have different feasible windows, transition costs, and resource-consumption patterns on different platforms, which increases the difficulty of unified modeling and efficient optimization. To address this problem, this paper proposes an evolutionary policy optimization framework for heterogeneous AEOS scheduling with preference-adjustable weighted objectives. In the modeling layer, assignment-based indirect encoding is combined with decoder-based equivalent-cost evaluation to retain satellite-dependent constraints while integrating task gain, energy saving, and load balance into an interpretable scalar utility. In the optimization layer, schedule decoding, population-based search, and online actor-critic operator control are decoupled, so that reinforcement learning selects high-level search operators rather than constructing schedules directly. Based on this framework, a reinforcement-learning-assisted operator-selection memetic evolutionary algorithm (RLOSMEA) is developed to coordinate global exploration, feasibility recovery, and local refinement under a limited function-evaluation budget. Experiments on different heterogeneous AEOS scenarios show that RLOSMEA achieves higher overall weighted utility and more stable convergence than representative metaheuristic baselines. Sensitivity and learning-behavior analyses further confirm the robustness of the proposed method and the effectiveness of reinforcement-learning-guided operator selection.

articles.title: Distance Is Not Enough: Forget-Retain Alignment Gap Predicts LLM Relearning Robustness
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.25429v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to make a model forget specific data, yet unlearned LLMs often fail to stay unlearned: brief fine-tuning can revive removed knowledge. Existing robustness predictors rely on global weight-space displacement, but distance alone can be misleading when random or destructive updates collapse performance. We argue that relearning robustness depends on update structure: robust unlearning should affect forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones. We introduce the Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), a training-free predictor that scores an update's forget-retain alignment without running a relearning attack, and separates selective from dense updates more reliably than global distance. Building on the forget-critical, retain-sparing principle, Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP) improves relearning robustness. Our results suggest that weight selectivity better explains robustness than distance alone. Code is available at https://github.com/Yi1-Chen/FRAG.

articles.title: Nested Convex-Body Chasing for Online Optimization with Evolving Feasible Sets
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.29074v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study online optimization with nested shrinking feasible regions in two settings: convex optimization with nested evolving feasible sets (CONES) and adversarial constrained online convex optimization (COCO). Our algorithms separate loss control from geometric movement: constrained minimizers and cumulative-loss tests preserve regret guarantees, while a deterministic resettable nested convex-body chaser limits movement.
  For CONES with a $G$-Lipschitz, $\mu$-strongly convex objective on a diameter-$D$ domain, we chase intersections of the current feasible set with adaptive objective sublevel sets. Using the Euclidean chasing ratio $O(\sqrt{d\log(1+d)})$, we obtain nonpositive regret at every prefix and movement $O(\sqrt{d\log(1+d)\,GD\log(eT)/\mu})$. The bound adapts to the increase in the constrained optimum value. In dimension two, with all other parameters fixed, every randomized algorithm with terminal expected regret $O(T^\beta)$, $\beta<1$, suffers $\Omega(\sqrt{\log T})$ expected movement on some deterministic nested sequence, proving optimal horizon dependence. Under linear growth away from the constrained minimizer set, Steiner-point tracking yields movement independent of $T$.
  For general convex COCO, one-step-delayed chasing with regularized-leader resets gives regret $O(G_fD\sqrt{d\log(1+d)T})$ and cumulative constraint violation $O(G_gD\sqrt{d\log(1+d)T})$. For strongly convex losses, both are $O(d\log(1+d)\log(eT))$ when other parameters are fixed. These reductions replace the $O(d^{d/2})$ projection-path factor in prior analyses by the polynomial dimension dependence of Euclidean nested convex-body chasing.

articles.title: Constructing and Evaluating Clinical Reasoning Trajectories for Medical Agent
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.05090v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Evaluation of medical artificial intelligence (AI) agents remains predominantly answer-centric, assessing only the correctness of final outputs while overlooking the quality of intermediate reasoning. We propose MedTraj, a framework that treats reasoning trajectories as primary objects for modeling the progressive refinement of clinical evidence toward diagnostic decisions. A reasoning trajectory captures the state transitions among medical concepts---from clinical observations through evidential reasoning to a final conclusion---making the implicit reasoning chain of a medical agent explicit and inspectable. Each trajectory is scored across five quality dimensions: coherence, evidence support, hallucination, completeness, and traceability. Controlled error injection introduces targeted faults into otherwise correct trajectories to establish causal links between specific reasoning failures and measurable quality degradation. Step-level filtering based on marginal contribution identifies which individual reasoning steps drive or undermine reasoning trajectory quality. Quality-weighted reasoning trajectory context feeds these evaluations back into the model at inference time. Experiments across CareQA, PubMedQA, and CECMed demonstrate that reasoning trajectory context consistently improves reasoning coherence. For the severity assessment on the CECMed, quality-weighted reasoning trajectory context nearly doubles the correctness over the zero-shot baseline while cutting the hallucination ratio by 87%. Experiments show that 15.3% of reasoning steps carry most of the quality signal, and that extending chains beyond four steps yields diminishing returns.

articles.title: Map Users and Mapmakers: The Scope of Cognitive Attribution from Acquired Representations
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.13879v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: An acquired representation can enlarge a system's cognitive repertoire without transferring the capacities exercised in producing that representation. This paper develops a framework for specifying that enlargement and its limits. Its central contribution is a five-part attribution table distinguishing effective tracking, application of acquired structures, acquisition from explicit specifications, acquisition from identifying observations, and retention and reuse. Each entry identifies a positive capacity commitment and a further claim requiring additional support. The argument deliberately grants meaningful content, causal efficacy, and productive inference, so that its conclusion does not depend on treating representations as inert encodings. Map and category examples show why even complete application competence leaves acquisition capacity undetermined, and why acquiring a criterion from its description differs from finding it in examples. Short formal proofs appear in an appendix. The framework is applied to Andrew Ng's world-model interpretation of Othello-GPT and to the specific indicators discussed in contemporary accounts of machine concepts. It preserves demonstrated recognition, classification, inference, and qualified acquisition while specifying what remains unestablished about criterion discovery and accumulation. The result concerns the scope of cognitive attribution rather than the constitutive conditions of concept possession: cognitive achievements deserve credit for the capacities they establish, without silently importing a broader repertoire through the labels attached to them.

articles.title: Who Audits Whom, on What Substrate, with What Evidence? An Independence-Graded Audit Protocol for Agentic AI
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.18272v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Agentic AI systems plan, invoke tools, and act with limited supervision; they are now both the subject of audits and, increasingly, the auditor. Independence-the foundation of assurance-is still applied to them as a binary. We argue that it must be graded along three orthogonal axes: principal independence (who controls the auditor), substrate independence (an auditor that shares the auditee's foundation-model family, toolchain, or guardrails fails with the auditee), and evidence independence (whether evidence is attestable rather than self-reported). Each axis has precedent; the contribution is to grade all three on a single audit, aggregate them by the weakest link, and apply the same rubric when the auditor is itself an agent. We give the model a formal basis by transplanting the beta-factor model of common-cause failure from reliability engineering. We also provide a seven-step protocol whose outputs a third party can verify, a structural detectability analysis of a procurement-controls agent audited at three grades, and a closed-form study of the model in which, at a declared common-mode share of 0.90 for a same-family auditor and a declared reporting probability of 0.6 for an internal team, a conventional internal audit of an agent-a real audit team, a second agent, and provider logs-surfaces 5.9% of the faults it could in principle see and, independently of those two values, none at all in half of the fault classes. Because an evidence grade says who could have altered a record, not what the record covers, every load-bearing record also carries a declared-scope predicate, and reports carry a false-flag rate beside the detection floor wherever the auditor's own performance has been measured. We map the triple to the EU AI Act as amended, ISO-IEC 42006, UK public-sector risk-management guidance, and audit-regulator practice.

articles.title: A Survey on the Linear Representation Hypothesis
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.22695v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The term "linear representation hypothesis" (LRH) has appeared across diverse subfields of artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and cognitive science. But previous works have not consistently treated the LRH as a falsifiable scientific hypothesis; we analyze these inconsistencies and examine their implications for how prior theoretical and methodological results should be interpreted. Based on this analysis, we argue that claims regarding linear representations become well-defined only through careful examination of the model, representation location, feature definition, and evaluation dataset. We therefore propose a more rigorous formalization of the LRH that makes these dependencies explicit and allows the hypothesis to be evaluated as a falsifiable scientific claim. Finally, we identify some non-trivial open problems that warrant further attention from the research community.

articles.title: Reliability Engineering for AI Systems: Challenges, Methods, and Directions
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.35316v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: AI reliability concerns whether an AI system performs its intended function dependably over a stated period and under stated operating conditions, with stated evidence. As these systems become more autonomous, that function includes more than a correct output. Retrieval, memory, tool use, permissions, human oversight, and interactions among systems must operate consistently and safely, and, for generative systems, so must the reasoning process that produces the output. Average benchmark accuracy measures capability; it does not quantify this broader reliability claim. This paper adapts established reliability engineering methods, from failure definitions and operational envelopes to FMEA, accelerated testing, field monitoring, and reliability growth, to AI systems. A four-level diagnostic framework classifies failures as component, operational-loop, agentic-conduct, or network and governance failures. Test, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV), sequential monitoring, and FRACAS create and refresh evidence. SMART provides statistical guidance for measurement, analysis, assessment, and test planning; the NIST AI Risk Management Framework provides organizational guidance for governance, evaluation, monitoring, and mitigation. Three cases illustrate the program: adversarial testing of a convolutional neural network, perception-error propagation, and autonomous-vehicle disengagements. Established reliability engineering provides a usable foundation; new measurements and safety guardrails are still needed as these systems are self-evolving.

articles.title: WISE-ATTA: When to Ask for Labels in Budgeted Active Test-Time Adaptation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.37687v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Active test-time adaptation (ATTA) improves robustness under distribution shift by updating a deployed model during inference while selectively querying supervision. However, most existing ATTA methods implicitly assume that supervision can be requested for every incoming test batch, which can incur substantial annotation cost over long test streams. In this work, we introduce budgeted ATTA in which labels are available for only a fraction of test batches. This formulation shifts the central challenge from deciding what to label within a batch to deciding when supervision should be applied over time. To address this challenge, we propose a budget-aware approach WISE-ATTA that allocates supervision over the test stream based on lightweight signals computed online, prioritizing periods where supervision is likely to be most useful. When a batch is selected for supervision, we further employ a drift-based sample selection criterion that targets samples exhibiting ongoing, unconverged adaptation dynamics, enabling effective updates from a single labeled example. We evaluate this approach on synthetic corruptions (ImageNet-C) and natural distribution shifts (ImageNet-R/K/A). Across settings, WISE-ATTA achieves competitive or improved performance compared to recent ATTA methods while requiring substantially fewer labels. Overall, we find that the timing of supervision is a key, yet underexplored, aspect of active test-time adaptation. Code: https://github.com/Muhammad-Huzaifaa/WISE-ATTA

articles.title: Aligned Data Can Induce Misalignment via Context Confusion
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.38379v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models are frequently updated for various use cases, where filtering out misaligned training samples is a common practice for preventing post-update misalignment. However, alignment is inherently context-dependent: a behavior that is aligned in one context may be inappropriate in another. For example, recommending that researchers retain their data for reproducibility is aligned, whereas recommending that a mobile app retain users' sensitive data may violate users' privacy. Starting from this observation, we identify a posttraining phenomenon where aligned training induces misaligned behavior in other contexts. We call this phenomenon context confusion. We demonstrate context confusion across three domains: (1) Gender Equality, (2) Privacy, and (3) Physical Safety. Unlike the broad misalignment seen in emergent misalignment, context confusion causes domain-specific misalignment that evades general alignment evaluations. Further, it is not effectively reduced by injecting general alignment training data, but can be substantially reduced by including targeted alignment data for the misaligned domain or providing in-context learning examples during inference. Lastly, we provide a mechanistic explanation of context confusion. We observe that queries from different domains can undergo similar representational shifts during the fine-tuning. Consequently, a query from a different domain may activate the same behavioral feature learned during fine-tuning, which causes the behavior to transfer to a context where it is misaligned. Based on our findings, we argue that it is difficult to predict the alignment state of a model after training by inspecting the training data alone, which highlights the importance of comprehensive post-training alignment evaluations.

articles.title: Component Replacement in LLM Agents: A Critical Scoping Review of Task Benefit and Attribution
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.39989v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Background: Choosing an agent controller and deciding which component to improve require different evidence. A replacement can change both the decision rule and what the agent can do after that decision. Objectives: We ask what existing replacement comparisons establish about task benefit and about attribution to local decision quality. Methods: This critical scoping review maps 348 studies and applies a five-step interpretation procedure to 94 comparison and diagnostic records from 42 studies, reading every inconsistent record against its source. Eight purposively selected cases illustrate the procedure. Results: The records comprise 33 executed task-outcome contrasts, 49 comparisons with restricted endpoints, and 12 diagnostic summaries. Only 14 task contrasts report contrast-level uncertainty, and the response policy is documented as retained in nine, all rule replacements from four studies; none of the 12 necessity-decision records executes a task contrast. Source checks distinguish whole-plan correctness, correct skill loading, and choice accuracy conditional on presentation from completed workflows. In Outcome Monitors, a count-matched timing placebo detects no timing effect (+0.88 points, 95% CI -4.39 to 6.14), so the source evidence attributes the detectable package gain to recovery content; detector selection at a fixed warning quota remains untested. Conclusions: The analysis separates evidence that can inform adoption from evidence that supports component development. Recovery and disruption, intervention timing, and downstream consumption organize three candidate mechanisms, and eight conditional reporting items specify the comparisons needed to distinguish the remaining explanations.

articles.title: Robust Nash Alignment under Preference Uncertainty
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.00715v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Preference-based alignment methods typically optimize against a single preference model, and can therefore be brittle when pairwise preferences are uncertain: noisy, heterogeneous, or shift after deployment. To address these issues, we propose Robust Nash Alignment, a game-theoretic framework for alignment to uncertain pairwise preferences. Our formulation has a major learner seeking a policy with a large worst-case win rate against both an adversarial competitor and any preference kernel lying in an ambiguity set around a nominal preference. When the ambiguity set captures the uncertainty in preferences, the resulting robust objective of the game directly yields a certified lower bound on worst-case performance. However, we note this problem is computationally challenging to optimize, and to address this, we introduce a four-player primal-dual proxy game involving the leader policy, follower policy, adversarial kernel, and dual variable, and develop a single-loop optimistic mirror descent-ascent algorithm for it. We show that the proxy always lower-bounds the truncated hard-constrained objective, quantify the proxy-to-hard gap, and characterize an exactness condition under which the proxy recovers the robust objective. We then prove an $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ average-iteration convergence for the proxy-game duality gap, which implies a near-optimal robust policy for the original robust objective. Experiments on controlled tabular games and LLM alignment with uncertain preference illustrate the method and show improved robustness to preference perturbations over nominal baselines.

articles.title: Interpreting at Write Time: A Policy Ablation for Multi-Goal Agent Memory
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.02897v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A long-running assistant cannot keep everything it has seen, so it summarises. Summarising is not neutral: what is kept depends on what the record is for, and the choice is made once, before anyone knows which of the user's goals will ask. We ask what a memory should summarise for when it serves several standing goals at once. Three write policies answer differently: summarise with no goal in view, write one summary covering every goal, or write one summary per goal and read them together. We compare them with five models, two short event streams and one LLM judge, holding the read step fixed. Answers from different goal stores overlap less than answers from one store on two runs, so the goals do pull apart. Per-goal summaries read together scored highest. They beat the all-goal summary on relevance, completeness and accuracy, but the neutral one only on relevance and completeness, and at matched answer length only on relevance. The all-goal summary scored below the neutral one, which had a quarter of its budget. A single goal store served its own goal's queries better than the other goal stores, but not better than the neutral summary.

articles.title: From Scientific Observations to Mechanisms: Benchmarking Hypothesis Generation by AI Scientists
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.05197v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Data-driven mechanistic hypotheses are essential to scientific discovery because they explain how underlying processes produce observed phenomena. AI agents and AI scientists increasingly support scientific data analysis. However, their ability to turn empirical findings into mechanistic hypotheses remains insufficiently examined. To address this gap, we introduce MechHypoBench, the first benchmark for evaluating whether AI agents and AI scientists can generate such hypotheses from empirical data. It combines paper-derived mechanisms from 14 scientific fields with real-world datasets containing 17.98 million records. The construction retains the observational complexity of empirical data while providing a specified underlying mechanism. Agents analyze the observations and propose open-form hypotheses. We develop an evaluation framework that assesses open-form mechanistic hypotheses through their consequences under withheld conditions. Experiments with general agents and AI scientists reveal a substantial gap between generated hypotheses and the underlying mechanisms.

articles.title: Can the Library Speak? Self-Advertised Method Selection for Formal Proving
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.09401v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM-based formal provers can retrieve relevant lemmas and prior proofs, but relevance alone does not say whether a mathematical method can be used on the current theorem. A method has prerequisites, a target, an intended action, and obligations that its use leaves to prove. Methods that look equally related to a theorem may therefore differ substantially in whether they offer a plausible next step. We formulate this as an applicability-aware method-selection problem and introduce self-advertisement: before candidates are ranked, a model generates a problem-specific proposal for each one, stating what part of the goal it targets, what action it would take, and what conditions that action requires. We organize 82 reusable methods from Putnam 2000-2014 as Method Contracts, which pair applicability descriptions with Mathlib anchors, a checked example or scaffold, and expected proof obligations. A single batched call elicits proposals across the library; vague or unsupported proposals are demoted, yielding a ranked shortlist accompanied by inspectable claims about each candidate's use. We analyze when similarity-based representations cannot distinguish methods with different applicability, how errors in applicability estimates affect shortlist quality, and what a checked scaffold guarantees under its stated assumptions. Against lexical, embedding, and embedding-plus-LLM reranking baselines, self-advertisement achieves 95.0% hit@5 on Putnam 2015-2025, compared with 84.2% for the strongest reranker. On IMO ProofBench, it achieves 91.7% compared with 88.3%. These results indicate improved coverage of annotated methods in the retrieved shortlists, particularly on Putnam.

articles.title: AliO: Output Alignment Matters in Long-Term Time Series Forecasing
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.11213v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Long-term Time Series Forecasting (LTSF) tasks, which leverage the current data sequence as input to predict the future sequence, have become increasingly crucial in real-world applications such as weather forecasting and planning of electricity consumption. However, state-of-the-art LTSF models often fail to achieve prediction output alignment for the same timestamps across lagged input sequences. Instead, these models exhibit low output alignment, resulting in fluctuation in prediction outputs for the same timestamps, undermining the model's reliability. To address this, we propose AliO (Align Outputs), a novel approach designed to improve the output alignment of LTSF models by reducing the discrepancies between prediction outputs for the same timestamps in both the time and frequency domains. To measure output alignment, we introduce a new metric, TAM (Time Alignment Metric), which quantifies the alignment between prediction outputs, whereas existing metrics such as MSE only capture the distance between prediction outputs and ground truths. Experimental results show that AliO effectively improves the output alignment, i.e., up to 58.2% in TAM, while maintaining or enhancing the forecasting performance (up to 27.5%). This improved output alignment increases the reliability of the LTSF models, making them more applicable in real-world scenarios.

articles.title: When a Conceptor Complement Becomes Gain: Operator Geometry and Behavioral Attribution in Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.16325v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: When a steering intervention changes a language model's behavior, which part of the intervention deserves the credit? We test this question for a target-centered, scaled conceptor complement by removing its fitted covariance filter while preserving the same target-specific center and gain. At the original aperture $\alpha=.05$ and gain $\beta=2$, all 21 fitted maps across three models and seven targets expand every direction at the generation intervention layers. The matrix correction is $0.093\%$--$7.815\%$ of the matched-control displacement on held-out extraction activations. In 480 paired comparisons within a 1,920-response study, retaining the matrix changes many individual texts but does not establish a consistent additional target-suppression benefit on the four-target panel. A geometric aperture sweep shows that the operating regime changes with the filter setting. Separately, an invertible soft filter preserves what an unrestricted affine readout can recover, whereas dedicated erasure methods reduce prediction by newly fitted probes. Together, the results show why a whole-intervention comparison cannot by itself attribute generated behavior to the fitted matrix: analyze the complete transformation, hold shared components fixed, and test its output consequences directly.

articles.title: Beyond Equation Search: Conjecture-Guided Discovery with SCOPE and ClosureBench
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.18938v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Most symbolic regression methods optimize candidate equations, but improving an equation's fit does not establish whether its underlying scientific conjecture should be retained, revised, or rejected. A conjecture may admit multiple mathematical realizations, and similarly accurate equations may imply different explanations. This motivates a shift from refining individual expressions to developing and testing the conjectures that guide them. We introduce SCOPE, a framework that sustains multiple conjecture-driven research trajectories. Multiple scientist agents independently pursue conjectures through equation modeling, question formulation, and active experimentation, then exchange evidence to revise their conjectures and research directions. Their findings are consolidated into a scientific report linking models, conclusions, and evidence. Existing equation-discovery benchmarks primarily assess recovered expressions, leaving the evidence and scientific conclusions established through the investigation underexamined. We therefore introduce ClosureBench, an interactive benchmark of 60 closure-discovery tasks across five scientific domains. ClosureBench focuses on closure-discovery tasks to give equation discovery a concrete scientific purpose. Each task embeds an unknown algebraic relation in a known PDE system, where agents control experimental conditions in OpenFOAM to acquire new data for equation discovery. Beyond equation accuracy, ClosureBench proposes three metrics to evaluate the discovery process: evidence faithfulness, mechanism insight, and experimental effectiveness. Compared with diverse baselines, SCOPE achieves higher equation accuracy on both ClosureBench and a real-world scientific discovery case, while producing more accurate, reliable, and effective scientific discoveries.

articles.title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.21791v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose \textbf{RSIFlow}, a \textbf{R}ecursive \textbf{S}elf-\textbf{I}mprovement framework that integrates adaptive work\textbf{flow} orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.

articles.title: FAOPs: Normal Forms and an Algebra for AI Agent Workflows
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.22061v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Organizations increasingly encode operational procedures as multi-step agent skills, here called Agent Operating Procedures (AOPs), that must be traceable, auditable, reproducible, access-controlled, and bounded in time and cost, as regulated sectors require. Yet AOPs are typically kept as coarse-grained files, in which steps bundle actions, copied procedures drift apart, any step may reach any tool, and refactoring goes unchecked. We present Functional Agent Operating Procedures (FAOP), a formal theory that brings database-grade discipline to AI agent workflows. FAOP recasts each workflow as a typed function over scoped state and subjects an entire library to four progressive normal forms: Decomposed (FNF-1) splits a workflow into atomic steps, Typed (FNF-2) makes its data flow explicit and type-checked, Factored (FNF-3) gives each shared sub-workflow a single canonical definition so a change propagates instead of drifting, and Scoped (FNF-4) checks that each FAOP lists resources used by its own actions and the FAOPs it calls, while guardrails declared by it and by FAOPs that call it remain attached to their sources. A FAOP algebra of provably sound equalities turns refactoring and parallelization into compiler rewrites; orthogonal extensions add optimization (+O), bounded completion with time and cost limits (+B), and reachability checks (+R); and an architectural-level classifier (0-3) determines whether a workflow needs AI at all. Together, these make integrity, isolation, typing, stopping limits, cost, and optimization compile-time concerns across the whole library, not runtime hopes. We implement the theory in SkillBase, an AOP management system (what PostgreSQL is to data, SkillBase is to AOPs), and a separate executor that loads FAOPs from SkillBase and enforces these guarantees at run time. A worked financial workflow illustrates the approach end to end.

articles.title: Stepwise Reasoning Verification: Don't Generate, Classify!
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.25441v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Verifying the reasoning of large language models is increasingly important as they are applied to complex mathematical and scientific problems. Existing work focuses on large decoder models and reports mixed results for generative and discriminative verifiers, leaving unclear which paradigm is more effective and whether large models are necessary. In this work, we cast stepwise verification as a natural language inference task: the problem and partial solution prefix form the premise, while the next reasoning step serves as the hypothesis to be classified as entailed or non-entailed. This formulation enables error localisation at individual reasoning steps and direct comparison of encoder classification, decoder classification, and decoder verdict generation across model scales and annotation budgets. Across five reasoning datasets, a 0.15B encoder classifier outperforms most generative verifiers with up to 4B parameters. On identical decoder backbones, classification outperforms generation from 0.5B to 4B parameters and matches it on the strongest 7B backbone---reaching comparable performance with roughly one tenth as many annotated problems. Our findings establish classification as a parameter- and data-efficient approach to stepwise verification and show that strong verification does not require large generative decoders.

articles.title: GraphEvoResearcher: A Cost-Matched Mechanism Analysis of Explicit Reasoning Graphs in Training-Free Self-Reflection
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.25978v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Training-free self-reflective protocols (generate, critique, revise) improve LLM reasoning but operate on a flat token stream: revisions cannot identify which prior step is unreliable, and stopping cannot exploit structural convergence. We introduce GraphEvoResearcher, a training-free protocol that lifts EvoResearcher's self-reflective meta-reward onto an explicit reasoning graph whose nodes are intermediate conclusions and whose typed edges encode support, contradict, and depends_on, with a graph-aware reward over correctness, efficiency, reflection, diversity, and structural signals. On deepseek-chat over GSM8K, MATH, and BBH (n=50 each), the protocol reaches 98%, 92%, and 82% in about two calls per question. Gains are significant against single-shot decoding on GSM8K and MATH and against flat reflection only on MATH; against cost-matched self-consistency the protocol is competitive, not dominant. A paired mechanism ablation over a shared response cache then shows what the graph contributes: holding model outputs fixed, neither the structural stop rule nor contradiction-driven repair changes which item is answered correctly, so the gains come from the forced second pass rather than from the structural reward. The ablation exposes the reason: the answer step never reads the edges it builds. We fix this with an edge-consulting arbitration step, which repairs one BBH item and fires on only 4% of questions, locating the binding constraint in how often construction declares conflicts. Testing the implied prediction on HotpotQA (n=100) falsifies it: the trigger rate does not rise with mul

articles.title: TimesJev: Thinking Fast on Time Series with System 1 Sufficiency
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.26002v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong potential for time series reasoning, while models that reason over time series are usually with long chains of thought. However, this process often consumes thousands of tokens, directly leading to substantial latency during inference. In contrast, System 1 models such as Jev make decisions instantly and can naturally be an alternative, but raw time series are not compatible with the embedding space of these models, thus hindering the reasoning performance, especially when input series contain thousands of numeric points. In this paper, we make a very early attempt to propose a time series System 1 model, namely TimesJev. Specifically, we first formalize System 1 sufficiency in time series reasoning, which motivates a compressed representation for time series with key frequency patterns preserved. To construct this representation, we derive a dimension reduction objective that combines (i) a sufficiency divergence that measures the core information lost during compression, and (ii) a realizability divergence that quantifies the incompatibility of the System 1 model to the optimal prediction given this representation. We optimize this objective by learning time series compression with a gating mechanism for sufficiency, and then aligning the selected representation with the embedding space for realizability. Finally, experiments on 13 datasets demonstrate that TimesJev outperforms reasoning models by over 62% with 62.9% less inference time than their fine-tuned versions on average.

articles.title: REFLEX: RNA Ensemble Generation via Flexibility-Calibrated Stochastic Bridge
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.26261v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: RNA molecules often function through multiple experimentally observed conformational states. A central challenge is to capture ensemble diversity without sacrificing structural fidelity: samples may collapse toward averaged representative structures or drift into unsupported conformational regions. We introduce REFLEX (RNA Ensemble generation calibrated by FLEXibility), a sequence-conditioned generator for RNA backbone-frame ensembles based on a heteroscedastic stochastic bridge on SE(3). During training, experimental B-factors calibrate residue-wise bridge widths, exposing each observed conformer through local perturbation neighborhoods with residue-specific scales while keeping constrained regions sharper. A learned flexibility condition guides the bridge-field network to recover target conformer-specific frames from these calibrated noisy states. At inference, REFLEX uses only the input sequence, requiring no MSA-subsampling heuristics. On a multi-conformer RNA benchmark, REFLEX achieves the best precision-recall trade-off for ensemble coverage across evaluation thresholds, while recovery-stress ablations indicate gains in target-frame recovery under stronger perturbations.

articles.title: PLE: Physical-Engineering's Last Exam
articles.summary:
