arXiv:2610.30537v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Frontier language models now score above 90% on popular knowledge benchmarks and are increasingly deployed as agents that carry out multi-hour professional work. Yet no existing benchmark tests whether they can perform the real-world, economically valuable work of a professional physical engineer, such as modelling physics and legal code requirements across a multi-format project corpus, optimising material and installation costs, and issuing 2D/3D engineering design packages that a licensed reviewer would sign off on. Existing engineering benchmarks focus on textbook question answering, isolated tool calls or self-contained toy design problems. As a result, most of these benchmarks are already saturated by leading agents and solving them is far away from delivering real engineering design. We introduce PLE, a benchmark of 85 long-horizon, agentic tasks in professional physical engineering consisting of electrical, civil, structural and mechanical engineering, where solving a task means completing a realistic, billable engineering deliverable. PLE combines two complementary curation paths. Expert-Authored tasks are created end to end by practising engineers from a professional data provider's expert pool. Co-Authored tasks start from problem statements written by practising engineers; an adversarial Creator-Solver agent pipeline constructs each task's realistic project environment, executable grader and reference deliverables before sending them to expert engineers for validation and difficulty intensification. We evaluate a variety of frontier LLMs under seven publicly available agent harnesses. Even the strongest configuration reaches a mean score of only 50.6%, while spending 27M tokens and 63 minutes per task on average, demonstrating the substantial gap between current agents and autonomous physical engineering design.

articles.title: PersonaScienceBench: Evaluating Scientific Agents with Diverse Simulated Researchers
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.32106v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scientific agents collaborate with researchers whose expertise and preferences differ, but benchmarks usually hold the collaborator fixed. We introduce PersonaScienceBench: 200 tasks from five benchmarks across four scientific domains. Simulated researchers provide context and feedback according to persona profiles, while task objectives and grading remain fixed. Agents encounter researcher preferences only through conversation. Across eighteen modelconfigurations, task performance, fact recovery, and self-repetition reveal different strengths. Detailed GPT 6 Astra analyses show distinct agent responses across researcher profiles; interaction traces illustrate targeted clar ification and workflow revision. These behaviors can differ even when final scores match. PersonaScienceBench therefore evaluates how agents collaborate with diverse researchers alongside whether they complete the task.

articles.title: Seeing the Options: What Should a Visual Candidate See?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.33702v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Agents often choose among candidates that are images: elements of a screenshot, product photos, charts. A single-pass decision model either encodes the request and all candidates as one sequence, making its answer depend on candidate order, or encodes each candidate alone, which keeps order invariance and reusable encodings but hides the request from the candidate. We ask where the joint encoder's advantage comes from: from candidates seeing the request, or from candidates seeing each other while they are encoded. With one backbone and the same fine-tuning steps on screenshot crops of Multimodal-Mind2Web, the answer is mostly the request. Continuing each candidate from a forked cache of the encoded request recovers 11 to 13 of the 12 to 17 points that independent encoding loses to joint encoding, at the price of cross-request reuse, and we prove that order invariance stays exact whenever candidates never see each other. A joint encoder retrained with its candidates isolated from one another during encoding loses 1.1 and 0.4 ranking points in one paired run (0.7 and 0.3 against the mean of five joint runs), and permutation-equivariant interactions among candidates, over pooled vectors or inside the encoder, gain nothing beyond continued training. At a matched abstention operating point the state-conditioned model is 0.6 and 1.0 points below the joint encoder (mean of four runs) with a flip rate of zero, against 8-10% for the joint encoder; on AndroidControl crops (three and five runs) it is 2.5 to 4 ranking points below. Finally, the abstention threshold drifts: the choice term of the loss ignores the score level, and the coverage term pins it only weakly once positives saturate; a quantile threshold aligns operating points.

articles.title: The Trinity: Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.36077v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

articles.title: Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.36116v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: \emph{why} should humans keep doing science, and \emph{how} should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is \emph{durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values}. From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, \emph{human understanding}, requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, \emph{human direction}, requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI's current limitations. And it judges each use of AI by its effects on human understanding and direction rather than by the type of tool, across every phase of research, including peer review and the training of new researchers. It closes with the reforms needed to keep science aimed at human understanding and direction.

articles.title: Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation and a Large-Scale Multi-SKU Benchmark for Shampoo Bottle Surface Defect Detection
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.38194v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Industrial shampoo-bottle surface defect detection must operate across many stock keeping units (SKUs), where differences in bottle geometry, material, label layout, reflectance, and imaging conditions can substantially alter the appearance of the same defect. Existing industrial defect datasets rarely provide both instance-level defect annotations and product-variant identities, making it difficult to study SKU-aware detection under realistic manufacturing conditions. We introduce Bottle-SKU, a large-scale multi-SKU benchmark for shampoo bottle surface defect detection. Bottle-SKU contains 13,119 images, 20,419 instance-level bounding boxes, seven defect categories, and 48 bottle SKUs, enabling evaluation of both shared defect recognition and SKU-specific appearance variation. To address the challenge of SKU-specific appearance variation, we propose Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation (ProDMM). ProDMM constructs a visual prototype for each SKU from training images and predicts a soft SKU distribution for each input. The resulting prototype-conditioned representation dynamically generates low-rank Query/Value modulation for the visual backbone and residual conditioning for defect-text-to-visual attention, while preserving the pretrained Grounding DINO detection pathway. The model is trained jointly with detection, SKU-domain classification, and modulation-regularization objectives. Experiments on Bottle-SKU and the public GC10-DET-SKU metallic surface defect dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of prototype-guided domain conditioning for industrial surface defect detection. The source code and model will be released on https://github.com/Event-AHU/Industrial_Anomaly_Detection

articles.title: Encode Once, Answer Many: Internalizing Context via Parametric Flow
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.38356v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models are typically adapted to a task either by placing knowledge in the input context, which keeps it external and re-encodes it on every call, or by fine-tuning, which internalizes it but demands a costly round of optimization per task. We aim to internalize the knowledge carried by a context directly into model parameters, without per-task optimization and without keeping the context in the input at inference time. To this end, we propose CLIK, a context-conditioned parameter generator that maps a given context to LoRA parameters for internalizing knowledge in a single forward pass through a Transformer encoder with cross-attention, requiring no test-time gradient updates. Once the generated LoRA is inserted into a frozen base model, the model answers downstream queries from the query alone, having internalized the context into its weights rather than re-reading it. Because the adapter depends only on the context, it is generated once and reused for every query on the same document, so the cost of reading that document is amortized across queries. On document question answering, CLIK substantially improves over the no-context base model and outperforms existing hypernetwork-based generators, while remaining behind a base model that reads the context directly, and it carries over to multi-turn dialogue without any multi-turn-specific training. Analysis further shows that the context-dependent part of the generated adapter concentrates in a compact and specific substructure.

articles.title: Accelerating Nonlinear MPC by Behavior Cloning with Separated Timescales: Application to Nuclear Reactor Load-Following
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.38496v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Behavior Cloning (BC) of expert controllers for multiscale dynamical systems is challenging: state variables evolving at widely separated timescales induce highly nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space may fail to adequately represent, degrading closed-loop generalization. We propose Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (SRLBC), an architecture designed to leverage the physical knowledge of multiscale systems in which slow state variables, fast (stiff) state variables, and predictable exogenous inputs evolve at different timescales. On 500 long-horizon roll-outs of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) load-following benchmark -a high-dimensional, stiff industrial system with challenging safety constraints -and across 20 training seeds, separated embeddings systematically outperform shared embedding baselines on cumulative cost, imitation accuracy and constraint satisfaction. The resulting standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at a computational cost 15 times lower on average. Since standalone policies still leave a few percent of trajectories infeasible, we embed the learned policies in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, in which the optimizer is only called when the predicted input sequence is not certified as safe. This yields controllers still 6.8 times faster than the NMPC controller on average, with a feasibility (i.e., constraint satisfaction) of at least 99.8% for all architectures, SRLBC retaining the lowest closed-loop cost. Under distribution shift, standalone BC policies degrade sharply: SRLBC degrades the least, and once safety-augmented, it retains a feasibility above 98% with the lowest closed-loop cost. Beyond the quantitative results, Jacobian-based sensitivity analysis shows that the resulting controller relies on a sparse and less redundant set of latent features, each attributable to a single group of physical variables, and aligned with the physical timescale decomposition of the system.

articles.title: KARMA: Training-Free Knowledge-Atomic Harness Evolution for Industrial Advertising Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.39884v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Industrial advertising agents must continually adapt their decision knowledge to changing product offerings, traffic patterns, and operating policies. We present KARMA (Knowledge-Atomic, Regression-Gated Modular Adaptation), a training-free framework that evolves six typed knowledge modules while keeping model weights and executable harness code frozen. During our evolution, a deterministic Trace Verifier maps observed errors to candidate modules, and a Critic compares successful and failed trajectories to guide a tool-constrained Evolver. The Evolver applies atomic knowledge edits, which a fixed validation gate retains only when their measured gain reaches a threshold; otherwise, the previous knowledge state is restored. We evaluate KARMA with three LLM families on cases sampled from a corpus of approximately half a million real-world operation logs across six e-commerce domains. Across 18 domain--model settings, KARMA raises the average hold-out score from 30.19 to 39.15 (+8.96 points, +29.7%). Ablations show that removing either successful or failed trajectories more than halves the average hold-out gain. Evolved knowledge also transfers across domains without further adaptation, yielding an average hold-out gain of 8.54 points across all source--target pairs. By linking retained patches to their diagnostic evidence and validation outcomes, KARMA supports inspectable, reversible knowledge adaptation for agents in Web marketplaces.

articles.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.40535v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost.
  In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography.
  In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system.
  RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.

articles.title: SAT-ACT: Learning CDCL Branching from Outcome-Derived Action Preferences
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.41290v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Learning-based approaches have increasingly been explored for SAT solving, with particular attention to improving branching decisions in conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) solvers. These approaches derive branching guidance either from static structural properties of SAT formulas or from dynamic signals obtained through solver feedback and execution traces. However, these forms of supervision provide limited evidence about state-dependent branching effects, while different outcome measures may favor different branching choices. To address these limitations, we propose SAT-ACT, an outcome-derived learning framework for CDCL branching. We design three complementary outcome comparison criteria to extract action preferences from independent branching action rollouts initiated at the same solver state. The criteria identify preferences supported by the outcomes and leave comparisons unresolved when the evidence is insufficient or conflicting, instead of forcing an ordering using a predefined scalar metric. A state-conditioned network learns branching priorities from the extracted preferences and uses them to guide CDCL search directly without online action rollouts. We further introduce non-dominated heuristic action supervision, which retains the solver-selected action as a training target only when it remains non-dominated under these preferences. Solver-level experiments show that SAT-ACT consistently reduces CDCL search costs on three SAT families and improves PAR-2 on the SAT Competition benchmarks.

articles.title: Specification-Guided Generation for Large Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.41511v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate structured outputs, but existing constrained-decoding methods mainly enforce syntax and cannot directly enforce satisfaction of a formal specification. We introduce a neuro-symbolic, specification-guided decoding framework that combines LLM generation with symbolic reasoning. At each step, the framework refines the decoding grammar by filtering out values that cannot be extended to an output satisfying the specification. We present a forward-only variant that guarantees specification satisfaction by construction, and a backtracking variant that revises earlier feasible choices when their downstream consequences leave only values that the LLM itself judges unsuitable. The framework is model-agnostic, requires no retraining, and builds on existing grammar-constrained decoding mechanisms. Experiments on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks show that the forward-only variant reliably produces specification-compliant outputs while reducing repeated LLM inference compared with rejection sampling and incurring modest symbolic-reasoning overhead. The backtracking variant further reduces cases in which the model is forced to select values that it has itself judged unsuitable, thereby substantially improving adherence to the LLM's stated interpretation of the prompt.

articles.title: Radial Kernel Attention for Global Feature Exchange in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.41675v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Existing approaches often rely on local neighbor graphs, which limit communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, whereas explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic computational cost. RKA maps interatomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their kernelized overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear complexity in the number of atoms for fixed feature dimensions. To ensure physically consistent predictions, we insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its dependence on radial coordinate . Our models are trained on official OPoly26 training set for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation set. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV (per-atom MAE of 0.1182 meV/atom) and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/Angstrom,improving all three metrics over UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. RKA provides a compact pathway for information exchange beyond local graph connectivity in polymer machine learning force fields.

articles.title: Understanding Certified Training with Interval Bound Propagation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2306.10426v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As robustness verification methods are becoming more precise, training certifiably robust neural networks is becoming ever more relevant. To this end, certified training methods compute and then optimize an upper bound on the worst-case loss over a robustness specification. Curiously, training methods based on the imprecise interval bound propagation (IBP) consistently outperform those leveraging more precise bounding methods. Still, we lack an understanding of the mechanisms making IBP so successful.
  In this work, we thoroughly investigate these mechanisms by leveraging a novel metric measuring the tightness of IBP bounds. We first show theoretically that, for deep linear models, tightness decreases with width and depth at initialization, but improves with IBP training, given sufficient network width. We, then, derive sufficient and necessary conditions on weight matrices for IBP bounds to become exact and demonstrate that these impose strong regularization, explaining the empirically observed trade-off between robustness and accuracy in certified training.
  Our extensive experimental evaluation validates our theoretical predictions for ReLU networks, including that wider networks improve performance, yielding state-of-the-art results. Interestingly, we observe that while all IBP-based training methods lead to high tightness, this is neither sufficient nor necessary to achieve high certifiable robustness. This hints at the existence of new training methods that do not induce the strong regularization required for tight IBP bounds, leading to improved robustness and standard accuracy.

articles.title: MindEye2: Shared-Subject Models Enable fMRI-To-Image With 1 Hour of Data
articles.summary:
arXiv:2403.11207v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Reconstructions of visual perception from brain activity have improved tremendously, but the practical utility of such methods has been limited. This is because such models are trained independently per subject where each subject requires dozens of hours of expensive fMRI training data to attain high-quality results. The present work showcases high-quality reconstructions using only 1 hour of fMRI training data. We pretrain our model across 7 subjects and then fine-tune on minimal data from a new subject. Our novel functional alignment procedure linearly maps all brain data to a shared-subject latent space, followed by a shared non-linear mapping to CLIP image space. We then map from CLIP space to pixel space by fine-tuning Stable Diffusion XL to accept CLIP latents as inputs instead of text. This approach improves out-of-subject generalization with limited training data and also attains state-of-the-art image retrieval and reconstruction metrics compared to single-subject approaches. MindEye2 demonstrates how accurate reconstructions of perception are possible from a single visit to the MRI facility. All code is available on GitHub.

articles.title: The Interpretable and Effective Graph Neural Additive Networks
articles.summary:
arXiv:2406.01317v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as the predominant approach for learning over graph-structured data. However, most GNNs operate as black-box models and require post-hoc explanations, which may not suffice in high-stakes scenarios where transparency is crucial. In this paper, we present a GNN that is interpretable by design. Our model, Graph Neural Additive Network (GNAN), is a novel extension of the interpretable class of Generalized Additive Models, and can be visualized and fully understood by humans. GNAN is designed to be fully interpretable, offering both global and local explanations at the feature and graph levels through direct visualization of the model. These visualizations describe exactly how the model uses the relationships between the target variable, the features, and the graph. We demonstrate the intelligibility of GNANs in a series of examples on different tasks and datasets. In addition, we show that the accuracy of GNAN is on par with black-box GNNs, making it suitable for critical applications where transparency is essential, alongside high accuracy.

articles.title: Expressiveness of Multi-Neuron Convex Relaxations in Neural Network Certification
articles.summary:
arXiv:2410.06816v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Neural network certification methods heavily rely on convex relaxations to provide robustness guarantees. However, these relaxations are often imprecise: even the most accurate single-neuron relaxation is incomplete for general ReLU networks, a limitation known as the *single-neuron convex barrier*. While multi-neuron relaxations have been heuristically applied to address this issue, two central questions arise: (i) whether they overcome the convex barrier, and if not, (ii) whether they offer theoretical capabilities beyond those of single-neuron relaxations. In this work, we present the first rigorous analysis of the expressiveness of multi-neuron relaxations. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that they are inherently incomplete, even when allocated sufficient resources to capture finitely many neurons and layers optimally. This result extends the single-neuron barrier to a *universal convex barrier* for neural network certification. On the positive side, we show that completeness can be achieved by either (i) augmenting the network with a polynomial number of carefully designed ReLU neurons or (ii) partitioning the input domain into convex sub-polytopes, thereby distinguishing multi-neuron relaxations from single-neuron ones which are unable to realize the former and have worse partition complexity for the latter. Our findings establish a foundation for multi-neuron relaxations and point to new directions for certified robustness, including training methods tailored to multi-neuron relaxations and verification methods with multi-neuron relaxations as the main subroutine.

articles.title: Smart Surveillance: Deep Learning and Hybrid Approaches for Dynamic Scene Analysis, Object Detection and Motion Tracking
articles.summary:
arXiv:2412.05331v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Event-triggered recording reduces the footage a surveillance camera must store, but the trigger decides how much idle video is kept, how many events are missed, and how much computation is spent. We compare six motion triggers (frame differencing, dense optical flow, MOG2, KNN, CNT, GSOC), a CNN detector, strided detection, and three motion-gated hybrids under one recording policy, on a benchmark of seven static-camera scenes (5,800 frames, 27 annotated events) with thresholds transferred to unseen scenes by leave-one-video-out. Detector-based triggers stored 19-28% of idle frames, against 36-89% for motion triggers. Under simulated camera jitter, frame differencing, optical flow, MOG2 and KNN stored 97-100% of idle frames, while detector triggers stayed below 29%. Running the detector on every 8th frame kept 99.7% of event frames at 9.8 ms of CPU per frame, cheaper and more robust than gating it with background subtraction. On VisDrone, raising YOLO11n's input from 640 to 1280 px raised AP from 15.5 to 26.8, more than a larger model, and INT8 quantization cut latency by 17% for 0.3 AP. In tracking, longer track memory raised IDF1 from 70.5 to 76.7, but every tracker recovered only 39-44% of overlapped people, because detection rather than association failed.

articles.title: Large Language Model Guided Self-Debugging Code Generation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2502.02928v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Automated code generation is gaining significant importance in intelligent computer programming and system deployment. However, current approaches often face challenges in computational efficiency and lack robust mechanisms for code parsing and error correction. In this work, we propose a novel framework, PyCapsule, with a simple yet effective two-agent pipeline and efficient self-debugging modules for Python code generation. PyCapsule features sophisticated prompt inference, iterative error handling, and case testing, ensuring high generation stability, safety, and correctness. Empirically, PyCapsule achieves up to 5.7% improvement in success rate on HumanEval, 14.6% on HumanEval-ET, and up to 24.5% on BigCodeBench compared to state-of-the-art methods. Notably, PyCapsule enables the open-source Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct 7B model to surpass the standalone performance of GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 on HumanEval and MBPP while requiring an average of fewer than 2 API calls per problem compared to up to 17 in competing frameworks. PyCapsule demonstrates broader impacts on advancing lightweight and efficient code generation, making competitive automated programming attainable with cost-effective, locally deployable open-source models.

articles.title: SQL-o1: Automatic Text-to-SQL Program Synthesis via Self-Reward Heuristic Search
articles.summary:
arXiv:2502.11741v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Efficient human-database interaction is a core problem in software engineering. Text-to-SQL (Text2SQL) tackles this by mapping natural language questions to executable SQL queries, enabling automatic SQL synthesis and reliable interaction. Although large language models (LLMs) have advanced significantly, current approaches struggle with poor transferability to open-source LLMs, limited robustness against logic and function errors in complex queries, and inefficiencies in structured search. We introduce SQL-o1, a self-reward-driven heuristic search framework built on an agent-based architecture to enhance model reasoning capabilities. SQL-o1 leverages Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for structured, multi-step exploration and incorporates a dynamic pruning strategy to accelerate inference without sacrificing accuracy. On the Spider and BIRD benchmarks, SQL-o1 achieves a 10.8-point execution accuracy improvement on the complex BIRD dataset, surpassing even GPT-4-based models. It exhibits strong few-shot generalization and robust cross-model transferability across open-source LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/ShuaiLyu0110/SQL-o1.

articles.title: Speculative Ad-hoc Querying
articles.summary:
arXiv:2503.00714v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) invite substantial effort and investment, yet agentic systems can spend much of their time waiting for tools. This paper explores how a small auxiliary LLM can reduce these waits by speculatively preparing a database while the primary LLM reasons.
  The challenge is that the auxiliary model must anticipate the primary model's actions before the primary model takes them. Our key insight is that database systems give the speculator a structural advantage: it need not predict the exact next query. Instead, it can prepare work shared by many plausible queries. Predicting query shapes enables advance compilation, predicting data access warms caches, and predicting broader data requirements enables precomputation of superset results that subsequent queries can refine.
  We present Wonder, a system that exploits this advantage for analytical SQL workloads. Wonder constructs reusable superset queries, materializes their components, and rewrites subsequent queries against the resulting temporary tables. Its scheduler prioritizes foreground queries while using reasoning intervals for speculative preparation. The same engine supports humans writing SQL, using incomplete queries to guide speculation and displaying intermediate results as they type.
  In a replay-based evaluation of agent workflows, Wonder reduces SQL execution time by up to 31.8% and combined primary-agent reasoning and active SQL time by up to 22.6%, with approximately 6% higher recorded main-agent and prediction API cost and 10% more read I/O on the full dataset. A separate 24-participant study finds significantly lower query latency on both analytical tasks and improved time-to-answer on one, with 87.5% of participants reporting increased productivity.

articles.title: Generative Learner for Distributional Causal Effects
articles.summary:
arXiv:2503.17894v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We propose a generative learner for estimating conditional average treatment effects and characterizing the full distribution of these effects. The learner takes the form of a multi-head feed-forward neural network with three jointly estimated subnetworks: the propensity score, the conditional quantile function of the baseline outcome, and the conditional quantile treatment effect. Each quantile-indexed subnetwork combines a covariate representation with cosine quantile embeddings through element-wise multiplication. We then recover the conditional average treatment effect as an integral over conditional quantile treatment effects. Under the classical causal assumptions within the Neyman--Rubin potential outcomes framework, we find that the proposed generative learner reduces out-of-sample mean squared error relative to the generalized random forest, double machine learning, and generative adversarial networks, with gains ranging from 5.4% to 93.5% on average across experimental designs. In an empirical application, we formalize the Stefan--Boltzmann law within a unidirectional causal model and apply the method to publicly available stellar data. The estimated effects satisfy the restrictions the law implies.

articles.title: Transferrable Surrogates in Expressive Neural Architecture Search Spaces
articles.summary:
arXiv:2504.12971v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) faces a challenge in balancing the exploration of expressive, broad search spaces that enable architectural innovation with the need for efficient evaluation of architectures to effectively search such spaces. We investigate surrogate model training for improving search in highly expressive NAS search spaces based on context-free grammars. We show that i) surrogate models trained either using zero-cost-proxy metrics and neural graph features (GRAF) or by fine-tuning an off-the-shelf LM have high predictive power for the performance of architectures both within and across datasets, ii) these surrogates can be used to filter out bad architectures when searching on novel datasets, thereby significantly speeding up search and achieving better final performances, and iii) the surrogates can be further used directly as the search objective for huge speed-ups.

articles.title: Narrative-Centered Emotional Reflection: An Early Prototype for AI-Supported Emotional Self-Reflection
articles.summary:
arXiv:2504.20342v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Reflexion is an AI-powered prototype designed to explore structured emotional self-reflection. By integrating emotion detection, layered reflective prompting, and metaphorical storytelling generation, Reflexion was intended to support users in autonomous emotional exploration beyond basic sentiment categorization. Grounded primarily in expressive writing, cognitive restructuring, and self-determination theory, the system was designed to organize reflection as a progressive pathway from surface-level emotional recognition toward value-aligned action planning. Its final action-planning layer is additionally informed by broader questions of agency and empowerment, which remain future directions rather than fully implemented mechanisms in the current prototype. Informal design feedback indicated that some reviewers found the layered interaction model understandable and potentially useful; no empirical efficacy claims are made. As an early prototype, Reflexion documents one direction in theory-informed affective computing. A public sample walkthrough of the four reflection layers is available at https://reflexion-2025-prototype.web.app. It uses fixed example outputs and no live AI analysis.

articles.title: Towards General Continuous Memory for Vision-Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2505.17670v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Language models (LMs) and their extension, vision-language models (VLMs), have achieved remarkable performance across various tasks. However, they still struggle with complex reasoning tasks that require multimodal or multilingual real-world knowledge. To support such capabilities, an external memory system that can efficiently provide relevant multimodal information is essential. Existing approaches generally concatenate image and text tokens into a long sequence as memory, which, however, may drastically increase context length and even degrade performance. In contrast, we propose using continuous memory, a compact set of dense embeddings to more effectively and efficiently represent multimodal and multilingual knowledge. Our key insight is that a VLM can serve as its own continuous memory encoder. We empirically show that this design improves performance on complex multimodal reasoning tasks. Building on this, we introduce a data-efficient and parameter-efficient method to fine-tune the VLM into a memory encoder, requiring only 1.2% of the model's parameters and a small corpus of 15.6K self-synthesized samples. Our approach CoMEM utilizes VLM's original capabilities to encode arbitrary multimodal and multilingual knowledge into just 8 continuous embeddings. Since the inference-time VLM remains frozen, our memory module is plug-and-play and can be flexibly integrated as needed. Extensive experiments across eight multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

articles.title: Learning to Charge More: How Q-Learning Firms Lock In Supracompetitive Prices
articles.summary:
arXiv:2505.22909v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: There is growing experimental evidence that $Q$-learning agents can learn to charge supracompetitive prices. We ask when such behavior persists, whether it emerges, and which strategies support it. In a repeated pricing game in which firms condition on the previous period's price profile, we give conditions on the learned action values under which supracompetitive prices become an absorbing state once experimentation ends. We then show that under softmax exploration these conditions are reached with positive and explicitly bounded probability, both from a random and from an all-zero initial $Q$-table. In the latter case firms lock in supracompetitive prices because they never learn that undercutting pays; the same mechanism can lock in the competitive price, so the long-run outcome is selected by the exploration path. Finally, we give sufficient conditions on the learned table under which the induced strategy is naive collusion, a grim trigger strategy or an increasing-price strategy; grim trigger strategies are subgame perfect under a standard discounting condition, whereas naive collusion is generally not an equilibrium.

articles.title: The Alignment Illusion: How BadReward Corrupts Text-to-Image Generation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2506.03234v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Modern text-to-image generative models increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to align generated content with human preferences and safety standards. This post-training stage is critical for optimizing models toward high-fidelity and value-aligned behaviors using human preference data. However, while previous works have extensively investigated poisoning attacks against the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage of text-to-image training, the security vulnerabilities introduced by the RLHF process remain unexplored.
  In this paper, we present the first exploration into the feasibility of poisoning the RLHF process as a novel attack surface for compromising text-to-image models. We introduce BadReward, an indirect clean-label poisoning attack that manipulates reward signals to embed malicious behaviors. Our approach leverages a feature collision mechanism to produce poison preference image pairs that are visually benign, but aligned with a malicious target concept in the reward feature space. Our experiments demonstrate that this manipulation effectively corrupts the reward signal. Online RLHF further amplifies this corruption through its reward-model feedback loop, whereas offline preference optimization learns directly from the poisoned preferences. Finally, we demonstrate the real-world effectiveness of BadReward on modern text-to-image architectures, showing high attack success rates and visual stealthiness across different RLHF algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJUICSR/BadReward.

articles.title: Tactile MNIST: Benchmarking Active Tactile Perception
articles.summary:
arXiv:2506.06361v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Tactile perception has the potential to significantly enhance dexterous robotic manipulation by providing rich local information that can complement or substitute for other sensory modalities such as vision. However, tactile sensing is an inherently local sensor modality, providing information only at the points of contact. This strict locality necessitates the use of active perception techniques to acquire useful, task-relevant information from manipulated objects or the environment in general. Hence, the agent must actively guide sensors toward regions with more informative or significant features and integrate this information over time to understand a scene or complete a task. While active perception and tactile sensing methods have received significant attention recently, both fields lack standardized benchmarks. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Tactile MNIST Benchmark Suite, an open-source, Gymnasium-compatible benchmark specifically designed for active tactile perception tasks, including classification, localization, pose estimation, and volume estimation. Our benchmark suite offers diverse simulation scenarios, from simple toy environments to complex tactile perception tasks using vision-based tactile sensors. Furthermore, we offer a comprehensive dataset comprising 13,580 synthetic 3D MNIST digit models and 153,600 real-world tactile samples collected from 600 3D-printed digits. Using this dataset, we train a CycleGAN for realistic tactile simulation rendering. By providing standardized protocols and reproducible evaluation frameworks, our benchmark suite facilitates systematic progress in tactile sensing and active perception more broadly.

articles.title: Multi-Scale Spectral Attention Module-based Hyperspectral Segmentation in Autonomous Driving Scenarios
articles.summary:
arXiv:2506.18682v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent advances in autonomous driving (AD) have highlighted the potential of hyperspectral imaging (HSI) for enhanced environmental perception, particularly in challenging weather and lighting conditions. However, efficiently processing high-dimensional spectral data remains a significant challenge. This paper presents an empirical investigation of a Multi-Scale Attention Mechanism (MSAM) for enhanced spectral feature extraction through three parallel 1D convolutions with varying kernel sizes (1-11) and adaptive feature aggregation. By integrating MSAM into UNet's skip connections, we evaluate performance improvements in semantic segmentation across multiple HSI datasets for urban driving scenarios. Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrate that MSAM consistently outperforms baseline UNet-SC, achieving average improvements of 2.32% in mIoU and 2.88% in mF1, while maintaining competitive GPU performance against established attention mechanisms. Our findings reveal that optimal kernel combinations are dataset-specific, with configurations such as (1;5;11) and (3;7;11) demonstrating particularly strong performance. This empirical investigation advances understanding of HSI processing capabilities for AD applications and establishes a foundation for adaptive multi-scale spectral feature extraction in automotive deployment.

articles.title: Autoregressive Image Generation with Linear Complexity: A Spatial-Aware Decay Perspective
articles.summary:
arXiv:2507.01652v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for image generation, as they can model visual tokens through the same next-token prediction principle that underlies large language models. However, most competitive AR image generators still rely on Transformer attention, whose quadratic token interaction cost and growing key-value cache become increasingly expensive for high-resolution visual sequences. Linear attention provides an attractive route to efficient AR generation, but our study shows that directly importing linear or decay-based attention from language modeling leads to clear quality degradation. We identify a key cause: after a 2D token map is flattened by raster scan, 1D sequence locality no longer faithfully reflects spatial locality, and conventional decay mechanisms may introduce a false-locality bias at row transitions. To address this problem, we propose Linear Attention with Spatial-Aware Decay (LASAD), a simple recurrent attention mechanism that modulates decay according to the original 2D token geometry while preserving linear complexity. Built upon this layer, LASADGen replaces standard attention in an AR image generator with spatial-aware linear attention. Experiments on ImageNet demonstrate that LASADGen achieves a favorable quality-efficiency tradeoff, improving generation quality over linear-attention baselines while reducing inference cost and memory usage compared with Transformer-based AR models.

articles.title: Large Language Models for Crash Detection in Video: A Survey of Methods, Datasets, and Challenges
articles.summary:
arXiv:2507.02074v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Crash detection from video feeds is a critical problem in intelligent transportation systems. Recent developments in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have transformed how we process, reason about, and summarize multimodal information. This paper surveys recent methods leveraging LLMs for crash detection from video data. We present a structured taxonomy of fusion strategies, summarize key datasets, analyze model architectures, compare performance benchmarks, and discuss ongoing challenges and opportunities. Our review provides a foundation for future research in this fast-growing intersection of video understanding and foundation models.

articles.title: A Formal Diagnostic Framework for Graph Repair Systems
articles.summary:
arXiv:2507.22419v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Graph-based data representations excel at capturing relations among entities, e.g., for semantic web, artificial intelligence, or database applications, and their utility depends critically on their quality, usually enforced via graph schemas. These schemas are often violated, e.g., during data ingestion, calling for repair actions to achieve compliance. This paper presents a formal diagnostic framework for graph repair methods. Current methods often lack rigor and generality, since they rely on ad hoc test datasets. Our method starts, instead, from a compliant graph and uses an abstract rewriting system to systematically introduce schema violations while ensuring provable coverage of the constraints in the schema. We apply the framework to several repair methods, including those based on large language models, and assess their performance across multiple metrics. Results show that our framework effectively differentiates the performance of different methods across various constraints, highlighting the importance of fine-grained, systematic tools for graph repair.

articles.title: Generative Logic: A Deterministic Reasoning Engine
articles.summary:
arXiv:2508.00017v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We present Generative Logic (GL), a deterministic computer architecture for automated mathematical reasoning. GL starts from axiomatic definitions written in a minimalist Mathematical Programming Language (MPL) and explores a configurable region of their deductive neighborhood. The definitions are compiled into a grid of Logic Blocks (LBs). An LB applies rules by hash-table lookups, and every statement it derives keeps its complete provenance. A run generates conjectures, removes those that counterexamples refute, tries to prove the rest, reduces the proved theorems to an essential core and writes every proof as navigable HTML. An independent verifier checks every proof step. From supplied definitions, GL derives the basic laws of Peano arithmetic and Gauss's summation formula. From previously proved lemmas, further definitions and a supplied list of conjectures, it builds a proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (FTA). These proofs are also exported to Lean 4 and checked by the Lean kernel. The next step is for GL to derive the FTA as well, without supplied conjectures. GL is designed together with a hardware architecture, the Mathematical Processing Unit (MPU).

articles.title: PrismServe: Efficient LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Accelerator Clusters
articles.summary:
arXiv:2508.09204v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Serving large language models across heterogeneous accelerators is challenging because partitioning a replica across device types introduces communication overhead during autoregressive decoding, while deploying complete quantized replicas can degrade model quality. We present PrismServe, a serving system that combines request-level collaboration across heterogeneous hardware with a mixture of quantized experts derived from the same foundation model. Each expert executes within a group of same-type accelerators in a single node, while a two-level router selects an expert based on predicted response quality and then selects a replica according to load and prefix-cache locality. Implemented on unmodified vLLM, PrismServe achieves 2.0--2.6$\times$ the throughput of cross-node or cross-vendor full-precision pipelined deployments and reduces P99 time per output token by 55--65\% when serving Qwen3-14B on 48 accelerators from three vendors. Across Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-32B on five downstream tasks, PrismServe outperforms the best single quantization method by 2.0--4.3 points while remaining within 1.4 points of full-precision accuracy. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LLM-Inference-System-B000/

articles.title: EAvatar: Expression-Aware Head Avatar Reconstruction with Generative Geometry Priors
articles.summary:
arXiv:2508.13537v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: High-fidelity head avatar reconstruction plays a crucial role in AR/VR, gaming, and multimedia content creation. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have demonstrated effectiveness in modeling complex geometry with real-time rendering capability and are now widely used in high-fidelity head avatar reconstruction tasks. However, existing 3DGS-based methods still face significant challenges in capturing fine-grained facial expressions and preserving local texture continuity, especially in highly deformable regions. To mitigate these limitations, we propose a novel 3DGS-based framework termed EAvatar for head reconstruction that is both expression-aware and deformation-aware. Our method introduces a sparse expression control mechanism, where a small number of key Gaussians are used to influence the deformation of their neighboring Gaussians, enabling accurate modeling of local deformations and fine-scale texture transitions. Furthermore, we leverage high-quality 3D priors from pretrained generative models to provide a more reliable facial geometry, offering structural guidance that improves convergence stability and shape accuracy during training. Experimental results demonstrate that our method produces more accurate and visually coherent head reconstructions with improved expression controllability and detail fidelity.

articles.title: SpecPrune-VLA: Accelerating Vision-Language-Action Models via Action-Aware Self-Speculative Pruning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2509.05614v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Pruning is a typical acceleration technique for compute-bound models by removing computation on unimportant values. Recently, it has been applied to accelerate Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model inference. However, existing acceleration methods focus on local information from the current action step and ignore the global context, leading to >20% success rate drop and limited speedup in some scenarios. In this paper, we point out spatial-temporal consistency in VLA tasks: input images in consecutive steps exhibit high similarity, and propose the key insight that token selection should combine local information with global context of the model. Based on this, we propose SpecPrune-VLA, a training-free, two-level pruning method with heuristic control. (1) Action-level static pruning. We leverage global history and local attention to statically reduce visual tokens per action. (2) Layer-level dynamic pruning. We prune tokens adaptively per layer based on layer-wise importance. (3) Lightweight action-aware controller: We classify actions as coarse- or fine-grained by the speed of the end effector and adjust pruning aggressiveness accordingly. Extensive experiments show that SpecPrune-VLA achieves up to 1.57$\times$ speedup in LIBERO simulation and 1.70$\times$ on real-world tasks, with negligible success rate degradation.

articles.title: Agentic Software Engineering: Foundational Pillars and a Research Roadmap
articles.summary:
arXiv:2509.06216v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Agentic Software Engineering (SE 3.0) represents a new era where intelligent agents are tasked not with simple code generation, but with achieving complex, goal-oriented SE objectives. To harness these new capabilities while ensuring trustworthiness, we must recognize a fundamental duality within the SE field in the Agentic SE era, comprising two symbiotic modalities: SE for Humans and SE for Agents. This duality demands a radical reimagining of the foundational pillars of SE (actors, processes, tools, and artifacts) which manifest differently across each modality. We propose two purpose-built workbenches to support this vision. The Agent Command Environment (ACE) serves as a command center where humans orchestrate and mentor agent teams, handling outputs such as Merge-Readiness Packs (MRPs) and Consultation Request Packs (CRPs). The Agent Execution Environment (AEE) is a digital workspace where agents perform tasks while invoking human expertise when facing ambiguity or complex trade-offs. This bi-directional partnership, which supports agent-initiated human callbacks and handovers, gives rise to new, structured engineering activities (i.e., processes) that redefine human-AI collaboration, elevating the practice from agentic coding to true agentic software engineering. This paper presents the Structured Agentic Software Engineering (SASE) vision, outlining several of the foundational pillars for the future of SE. The paper culminates in a research roadmap that identifies a few key challenges and opportunities while briefly discussing the resulting impact of this future on SE education. Our goal is not to offer a definitive solution, but to provide a conceptual scaffold with structured vocabulary to catalyze a community-wide dialogue, pushing the SE community to think beyond its classic, human-centric tenets toward a disciplined, scalable, and trustworthy agentic future.

articles.title: Functional Critics for Off-Policy Actor-Critic: From Stability to Exploration
articles.summary:
arXiv:2509.22964v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Actor-critic methods are central to modern reinforcement learning, yet off-policy actor-critic theory remains far removed from practical algorithms, due in part to the interaction between the deadly triad and the continually changing target policy. We revisit functional critics, i.e., value functions that explicitly condition on the policy, and show that this representation provides a shared foundation for off-policy training stability and policy-space exploration. We first develop a convergent off-policy actor-critic framework under linear function approximation that accommodates target-based TD, partial coverage, and evolving behavior policies. Our analysis combines a policy-evaluation guarantee under partial coverage with policy-gradient generalization of functional critics to yield a dual trust-coverage framework that controls policy-gradient error under evolving behavior policies while enabling greater reuse of off-policy data. We further develop a replay-buffer analysis under i.i.d. sampling, yielding a principled replay-sampling design for minimizing the replay-sample complexity required to reach a prescribed evaluation accuracy. We next show that functional critics provide a natural representation for model-free posterior-sampling-style exploration. Standard critic ensembles do not naturally represent joint uncertainty over return functions across policy space, whereas functional-critic ensembles represent policy-conditioned return functions directly. This motivates a particle-based, model-free analogue of posterior-sampling-style exploration without explicit model learning. Finally, we instantiate these ideas in a deep functional actor-critic algorithm that, despite omitting several standard off-policy AC heuristics, achieves strong performance across the full Dog and Humanoid task series of the DeepMind Control Suite.

articles.title: DELTA: Robustly Training Label-Conditional Diffusion Models with Weak Annotations
articles.summary:
arXiv:2510.03016v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: While label-conditional diffusion models have recently exhibited remarkable generative capabilities, their success heavily relies on massive, cleanly labeled datasets. In practice, categorical supervision is rarely perfect: it is often corrupted by noise, clouded by ambiguity, or partially missing. Training directly on such weak annotations severely degrades generation quality, and existing robust methods offer only fragmented solutions that depend on scarce auxiliary priors. To overcome these limitations, we propose DELTA, a unified framework that robustly trains Diffusion modELs across all three weak annoTAtion types. By treating the unknown true label as a latent variable, DELTA optimizes a principled variational objective that jointly recovers the clean data distribution and infers the true label posteriors. To make this joint training computationally tractable, we further introduce a median-centered timestep sampling strategy that efficiently concentrates estimation where the diffusion process is most informative. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that DELTA produces high-fidelity, class-consistent samples across diverse weak supervision scenarios, outperforming specialized baselines while demanding strictly less prior knowledge.

articles.title: AgentTypo: Adaptive Typographic Prompt Injection Attacks against Black-box Multimodal Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2510.04257v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal agents built on large vision-language models are increasingly deployed in open-world settings but remain highly vulnerable to prompt injection. Typographic text-in-image attacks such as FigStep have been evaluated mainly on standalone vision-language models. For agents, user goals, webpage context, and action history make the effect of embedded instructions uncertain, and robustness to behavior-guided, adaptive visual injections remains insufficiently studied. We introduce AgentTypo, a black-box red-teaming framework that launches adaptive typographic prompt injection by embedding optimized text into webpage images. We formulate an attention-guided automatic typographic prompt-injection objective that favors the attacker's expected answer over the clean-page answer, together with task-conditioned visual attention from small question-answering models. A novel black-box optimization method searches text position, contrast, and color. To further strengthen the attack, we develop a multi-LLM system that iteratively refines injection prompts using evaluation feedback and retrieves successful past examples for strategy learning. Experiments on the VWA-Adv and Mind2Web benchmarks show that AgentTypo significantly outperforms state-of-the-art image-based prompt injection attacks. Across seven closed- and open-source model backends, AgentTypo-pro achieves 45%-83% ASR, outperforming the CLIP-based AgentAttack by 29-47% and previous typographic attacks by 25%-37% on VWA-Adv.

articles.title: On the Structure of Stationary Solutions to McKean-Vlasov Equations with Applications to Noisy Transformers
articles.summary:
arXiv:2510.20094v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study stationary solutions of McKean-Vlasov equations on the circle. We establish an exact equivalence between solutions of the stationary McKean-Vlasov equation and an infinite-dimensional quadratic system of equations over Fourier coefficients, allowing explicit characterization of stationary states in a sequence space rather than a function space. This framework provides a transparent description of local bifurcations, their periodicity and resonance structures, while accommodating singular potentials. We derive analytic expressions for the emergence, form and shape (supercritical, critical, subcritical or transcritical) of bifurcations involving possibly multiple Fourier modes and connect them with discontinuous phase transitions. We also characterize, under suitable assumptions, the detailed structure of the stationary bifurcating solutions through leading small-amplitude coefficients for arbitrarily many fixed Fourier modes. At the global level, we establish regularity and concavity properties of the free energy landscape, proving existence, compactness, and coexistence of globally minimizing stationary measures, and identifying discontinuous phase transitions with points of non-differentiability of the minimum free energy map. We apply the theory to the Noisy Mean-Field Transformer model, where we show how changing the inverse temperature $\beta$ affects the geometry of the infinitely many bifurcations from the uniform measure. We also discuss how increasing $\beta$ motivates the study of approximate multi-mode stationary profiles as candidates for a separate metastability analysis; persistence times require additional dynamical estimates. Moreover, we determine the exact threshold $\beta_0\simeq2.447$ separating continuous and discontinuous phase transitions in this model. The same threshold marks the change of the first bifurcation from supercritical to subcritical.

articles.title: AuthRank: Scoring Source Credibility to Counter Poisoning in CTI LLM Pipelines
articles.summary:
arXiv:2510.20768v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) pipelines have become essential for processing Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) to quickly extract updated threat information from open source feeds and reports for real time processing. However, these pipelines are susceptible to poisoning attacks, and previously proposed defenses can fail for CTI contexts as cyber threat information is often completely novel, and attackers can easily mimic the stylistic conventions. We propose that the robustness of LLM pipelines can be improved by applying source credibility algorithms on document corpora, using PageRank as an example. We introduce AuthRank, a credibility score computed from citation networks built using explicit citations, LLM-inferred citations, and claim-level entailment, enhanced with time decay and author credibility. Our experiments on the standardized MS MARCO dataset demonstrate improved accuracy under poisoning, and we show proof-of-concept performance on CTI documents and feeds.

articles.title: TempoPFN: Synthetic Pre-training of Linear RNNs for Zero-shot Time Series Forecasting
articles.summary:
arXiv:2510.25502v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Foundation models for zero-shot time series forecasting face challenges in efficient long-horizon prediction and reproducibility, with existing synthetic-only approaches underperforming on challenging benchmarks. This paper presents TempoPFN, a univariate time series foundation model based on linear Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) pre-trained exclusively on synthetic data. The model uses a GatedDeltaProduct architecture with state-weaving for fully parallelizable training across sequence lengths, eliminating the need for windowing or summarization techniques while maintaining robust temporal state-tracking. Our comprehensive synthetic data pipeline unifies diverse generators, including stochastic differential equations, Gaussian processes, and audio synthesis, with novel augmentations. In zero-shot evaluations on the Gift-Eval, fev-bench and Chronos-ZS benchmarks, TempoPFN achieves top-tier competitive performance, surpassing the majority of models trained on real-world data, while leveraging fully parallelizable training and inference. We open-source our complete data generation pipeline and training code, providing a reproducible foundation for future research.

articles.title: AQBuc: Air Pollution Forecasting in Bucharest
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.00532v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In recent years, air pollution, especially the particulate matter $2.5\,\mu\text{m}$ (PM2.5), has become a growing concern mainly in urban areas. Exposure to air pollution is linked to the development of numerous health conditions, such as the aggravation of respiratory diseases, cardiovascular disorders, impaired lung function, and even cancer or early death. Forecasting future levels of PM2.5 has become increasingly important, as it can provide early warnings and help prevent diseases. We propose AQBuc, a dataset for predicting PM2.5 pollution in Bucharest, Romania, introducing an understudied location, as most work in this field has focused on Asian cities. Our dataset allows us to benchmark models for predicting future levels of PM2.5 across various time horizons. We evaluate a broad range of methods, including machine learning models, such as linear regression and ensemble-based methods, deep learning models based on recurrent networks and transformers, and large language models (LLMs). Specialized time-series models handle temporal data better, especially on longer horizons, while tree ensembles are more cost-effective for short horizons. Meanwhile, LLMs struggle to capture continuous sensor dynamics without specialized architectural changes.

articles.title: MAESTRO: Orchestrating Robotics Modules with Coding Agents for Zero-Shot Generalist Robots
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.00917v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Today's dominant route to generalist robots scales robotics data to train end-to-end policies. We instead use a vision-language model (VLM) as a coding agent that writes robot programs using a curated library of perception, planning, and control tools. MAESTRO's orchestration harness packages multi-step perception and action procedures into callable tools and guides their use through a plan-act-replan loop, using visual and execution feedback to verify outcomes and recover from failures. With this tool library and harness, MAESTRO matches or surpasses state-of-the-art vision-language-action (VLA) models zero-shot in our tabletop comparison and performs diverse mobile manipulation tasks, without collecting new teleoperation data or invoking a VLA tool. Ablations show that expanding the tool library improves average task progress with the full harness, while adding tools without it does not reliably improve progress. Case studies illustrate MAESTRO's potential for autonomous code improvement across trials, faster execution with VLA tools, and automatic robot data generation. We show that expanding robotics tool libraries together with their orchestration harnesses offers a complementary route to general-purpose robots alongside scaling end-to-end robot training data. Project site: https://maestro-robot.github.io. Code: https://github.com/penn-pal-lab/maestro.

articles.title: ScenicProver: A Framework for Compositional Probabilistic Verification of Learning-Enabled Systems
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.02164v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Full verification of learning-enabled cyber-physical systems (CPS) has long been intractable due to challenges including black-box components and complex real-world environments. Existing tools either provide formal guarantees for limited types of systems or test the system as a monolith, but no general framework exists for compositional analysis of learning-enabled CPS using varied verification techniques over complex real-world environments. This paper introduces a tool, ScenicProver, that aims to fill this gap by enabling the construction of sound, formally-checked assurance cases for CPS. ScenicProver is backed by a formal theory, which we lay out in this paper. ScenicProver supports: (1) environment modeling using the Scenic probabilistic programming language; (2) compositional system modeling with clear component interfaces, ranging from interpretable code to black boxes; (3) assume-guarantee contracts over those components using an extension of Linear Temporal Logic containing arbitrary Scenic expressions; (4) evidence generation through testing, formal proofs in Lean 4, and external assumptions; (5) sound combination of generated evidence using contract operators with Pacti; and (6) automatic generation of assurance cases tracking the provenance of system-level guarantees. We demonstrate its effectiveness through two case studies: one on an automatic emergency braking system with sensor fusion and one on drone safety. By leveraging manufacturer guarantees for sensors and focusing testing effort on uncertain conditions, our approach enables stronger probabilistic guarantees than monolithic testing with the same computational budget.

articles.title: InTAct: Interval-based Task Activation Consolidation for Continual Learning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.17439v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Continual learning seeks to acquire new knowledge while preserving previously learned representations. Despite the success of prompt-based methods, they remain fragile in domain-incremental learning scenarios, where shifts in the input distribution cause representation drift in shared layers and lead to forgetting. We introduce InTAct, a method that preserves functional behavior in shared representations without freezing parameters or retaining past data. InTAct constrains updates within activation regions associated with prior domains, while allowing flexible adaptation elsewhere, thereby stabilizing neuron functionality rather than directly restricting parameter values. The approach is architecture-agnostic, integrates seamlessly with existing prompt-based frameworks, and matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods on domain-incremental benchmarks.

articles.title: Beyond MACs: Deployment-Constrained Design Space Exploration for Tensorized Neural Networks
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.17971v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Tensor-train (TT) compression reduces neural-network parameters, but the latency of a tensorized layer is set by its contraction order and its mapping onto hardware: a contraction path with fewer multiply-accumulate operations (MACs) is not necessarily faster on a systolic array. We present a deployment-constrained, latency-guided design space exploration (DSE) framework for fixed-rank tensorized neural networks (TNNs) under a fixed processing-element (PE) budget. Using MAC-guided path pruning, it evaluates feasible combinations of contraction paths, three PE-array partitions, and input-, output-, and weight-stationary dataflows. By minimizing the sum of inference and training latency estimates, it selects a single physical PE partition shared across layers and both modes, while allowing layer- and mode-specific paths and dataflows. On ResNet-18 and ViT-Ti/4, 25%-50% of the layers select a path other than the minimum-MAC one, the best dataflow varies across layers and models, and on a representative ViT layer the latency-selected candidate reduces simulated latency by 23.5% relative to the minimum-MAC candidate. Deployed on a Xilinx VU9P FPGA accelerator that supports both inference and training, the complete TT+INT8 system achieves 3.28x-4.00x inference and 3.42x-3.85x training speedups over dense implementations with the same PE budget.

articles.title: Prompt Less, Smile More: Semantic Engineering in Lieu of Prompt Engineering
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.19427v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: AI-integrated applications increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs), but their intended behavior is not always fully specified by code. Meaning Typed Programming (MTP) automates prompt construction from program structure, yet selection criteria, output requirements, and application policies can remain unstated. We introduce Semantic Engineering, a methodology for identifying such missing intent and selectively adding and refining model guidance. We realize this methodology through Semantic Context Annotations (SemTexts), a dedicated language mechanism independent of documentation and schema metadata. SemTexts associate natural-language instructions with individual program entities and use declaration scopes to determine where they apply. Our implementation extends the Jac compiler and MTP runtime to preserve these associations and select applicable guidance during automatic prompt construction. We evaluate Semantic Engineering on seven AI-integrated applications and two standard benchmarks across three models. Across the applications, it achieves a 5.46-fold reduction in integration lines of code relative to Prompt Engineering while delivering equal or better task performance in most model-application settings, reaching up to 1.83 times the task performance of Prompt Engineering.

articles.title: Dual Randomized Smoothing: Beyond Global Noise Variance
articles.summary:
arXiv:2512.01782v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Randomized Smoothing (RS) is a prominent technique for certifying the robustness of neural networks against adversarial perturbations. With RS, achieving high accuracy at small radii requires a small noise variance, while achieving high accuracy at large radii requires a large noise variance. However, the global noise variance used in the standard RS formulation leads to a fundamental limitation: there exists no global noise variance that simultaneously achieves strong performance at both small and large radii. To break through the global variance limitation, we propose a dual RS framework which enables input-dependent noise variances. To achieve that, we first prove that RS remains valid with input-dependent noise variances, provided the variance is locally constant around each input. Building on this result, we introduce two components: (i) a variance estimator predicts an optimal noise variance for each input, (ii) this estimated variance is then used by a standard RS classifier. The variance estimator is independently smoothed via RS to ensure local constancy, enabling flexible design. We also introduce training strategies to iteratively optimize the two components. Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that our dual RS method provides strong performance for both small and large radii-unattainable with global noise variance-while incurring only a 60% computational overhead at inference. Moreover, it outperforms prior input-dependent noise approaches across most radii, with gains at radii 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0 of 15.6%, 20.0%, and 15.7%. On ImageNet, dual RS remains effective across all radii, with advantages of 8.6%, 17.1%, and 9.1% at radii 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5. Additionally, the dual RS framework provides a routing perspective for certified robustness, improving the accuracy-robustness trade-off with off-the-shelf expert RS models.

articles.title: PerNodeDrop: A Method Balancing Specialized Subnets and Regularization in Deep Neural Networks
articles.summary:
arXiv:2512.12663v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Deep neural networks possess strong representational capacity yet remain vulnerable to overfitting, primarily because neurons tend to co-adapt in ways that, while capturing complex and fine-grained feature interactions, also reinforce spurious and non-generalizable patterns that inflate training performance but reduce reliability on unseen data.
